articles.title: Taiwan’s New F-16s: Why They Still Matter
articles.full_text:
The Republic of China Air Force waited 20 years for these aircraft. What are they for?
Air Force Reserve Crews over Southern California with the 370th FLTS from Edwards Air Force Base provide aerial refueling from a KC-135 to a Lockheed Martin F-16 Block 70 aircraft for the Royal Bahraini Air Force in 2024.
The arrival of the first pair of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 aircraft on order to the Republic of China Air Force (ROCAF) has been a long time coming – and not just because of production delays. First sought as 66 F-16C/Ds under U.S. President George W. Bush, the request was blocked by his administration and remained unapproved under President Barack Obama, before the sale was signed off in 2019 during the first term of President Donald Trump. Yet their arrival comes after years of debate over whether Taiwan’s vulnerable air bases could sustain fighter operations in wartime, raising questions over what role the aircraft can realistically play.
Taiwan’s F-16 story begins in the 1970s. During that decade, it was quickly becoming clear that the island’s fleet of F-100 and F-104 combat aircraft was heading toward obsolescence. While agreement had been reached between Washington and Taipei for the co-production of the upgraded F-5E/F for the ROCAF, many U.S. officials themselves regarded additional F-5Es as inadequate as a long-term solution. Complicating any follow-on agreements, however, was the steady reconciliation between the U.S. and mainland China. 
In 1978, Taipei’s request for F-16s was dismissed out of hand, leaving the F-4 and additional F-5E/Fs as the main options. A decision that year settled on the latter. High-performance fighters again topped Taiwan’s arms requests the following year, but Washington maintained its refusal to supply the F-4, F-16, or F-18.
In December 1978, Washington announced that diplomatic recognition would shift to Beijing on January 1, 1979, and formally gave the one-year notice required to terminate the U.S.-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty, which became defunct on January 1, 1980. This appeared to close the door on a major new fighter sale, despite the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act specifying that it was U.S. policy “to provide Taiwan with arms of a defensive character,” although what sales that required would be determined by the President and Congress. 
Washington repeatedly calibrated Taiwan’s fighter access to its assessment of China’s capabilities and to the wider U.S.-China relationship. Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election campaign featured positive rhetoric toward Taiwan. However, after considering Taiwan’s requests for the F-5G (which would become the F-20) and the F-16/79 (a deliberately lower-performance export version of the F-16), the decision was once again made to reject the request and focus on the F-5E/F, as well as giving authorization for the transfer of used F-104 fighters from West Germany. Washington judged the F-5E/F qualitatively adequate against China’s then-current fighters.
Reagan institutionalized the arms sales problem in 1982, when the Third Communiqué between Washington and Beijing featured a pledge that arms sales to Taiwan would not exceed recent levels, with Washington stating that it intended to gradually reduce them over time, conditional on Beijing’s continued peaceful approach to the Taiwan issue. At the same time, the Six Assurances issued to Taipei sought to confirm that the U.S. had not agreed to set a date for ending arms sales, but the communiqué nonetheless remained part of the U.S.-China policy framework. At this point, Taiwan began the journey down alternative aircraft procurement paths, including what eventually became the F-CK-1 Indigenous Defense Fighter, produced with extensive assistance from U.S. industry.
However, the end of the Cold War once again changed the dynamic, and in September 1992, during his re-election campaign,  George W. Bush signed off on the purchase by Taiwan of 150 F-16A/B aircraft. The decision was in part justified by China’s purchase of Russian Su-27 aircraft. Domestic politics also favored the decision: General Dynamics built the F-16 in Fort Worth, and Bush announced the sale there during an election campaign in which Texas aerospace employment was politically salient.
Washington continued to approve substantial arms sales to Taiwan over the following decades. From 2006, however, Taipei’s campaign for 66 new F-16C/Ds repeatedly foundered amid changing U.S. concerns that included Taiwan’s own defense budgeting, cross-Strait stability and the broader U.S.-China relationship. The Obama administration instead approved a major upgrade of 145 of the ROCAF’s existing F-16A/Bs. Taiwan also continued to explore a more radical solution to its future fighter requirement: in March 2018, Defense Minister Yen Teh-fa said that future aircraft should ideally possess short-takeoff-and-landing capabilities, identifying the F-35B as one possible candidate. However, attention was increasingly shifting back toward new (and more obtainable) F-16s, and the Trump administration approved the sale of the aircraft the following year.
The backdrop to this was an increasing appreciation that the ROC would not be able to match the PRC on a system-for-system basis. This included combat aircraft, which were also thought particularly vulnerable as their reliance on large, fixed bases left them exposed to being destroyed or trapped on the ground – a concern that likely contributed to Taiwan’s interest in the less runway-dependent F-35B. While Taiwan possesses an extensive network of hardened and underground aircraft shelters, and has practiced operations from roadways, the volume of precision fire the PLA could be expected to deliver would mean the ROCAF would struggle to sustain operations. 
Reflecting this, Taiwan’s wider defense strategy and procurement priorities have also evolved. The “Hard ROC” concept of the late 2000s emphasized hardening, survivability and denying China a quick victory, even as Taipei continued to seek major conventional systems such as new F-16s. Admiral Lee Hsi-ming’s Overall Defense Concept, launched in 2017, pushed related ideas substantially further by placing much greater emphasis on force preservation and asymmetry. Elements of both – particularly force preservation, resilience and asymmetric capability – are now visible in contemporary strategy. The procurement patterns of the 2020s have also reflected the asymmetry requirement, with truck-based anti-ship missiles, HIMARS rocket launchers, anti-tank missiles and mobile surface-to-air missiles receiving major funding. 
During Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv’s air force confounded expectations by not only surviving but continuing to operate through the dispersal of its assets away from major bases and wider efforts at concealment. However, while we cannot be sure of the maturity or effectiveness of China’s precision strike kill web in advance of a conflict, evidence indicates both a much larger precision-missile arsenal with a more persistent surveillance network than that available to Moscow in 2022. Taiwan’s limited size and proximity to the mainland leave restricted scope for defensive countermeasures. The 2026 conflict with Iran has provided another warning of the challenge the island faces, with repeated missile and drone attacks by Tehran demonstrating the vulnerability of bases sited in close proximity to an opponent with a precision strike capability. 
So, the question becomes: if Taiwan already has modernized F-16s, and a substantial body of defense analysis argues that conventional fighters would play only a limited role during the opening phase of an all-out war, why buy new aircraft at all? 
The biggest difference is also the simplest: the new aircraft will supplement an existing fleet that has seen decades of use. While possessing the same radar as the older upgraded aircraft, the F-16 Block 70 does have some real advantages over the upgraded fleet. More powerful engines and a greater range and endurance, thanks to conformal fuel tanks mounted on the fuselage (the ROCAF possesses no aerial-refueling tankers), make them more capable in the interception, patrol, reconnaissance (particularly when fitted with the new MS-110 multispectral pod), and strike roles. The aircraft should also be more survivable once airborne than their predecessors, as they are intended to be fitted with the AN/ALQ-254 Viper Shield enhanced electronic warfare suite – although reports indicate this capability has not yet been installed due to production delays. A structural service life of 12,000 hours is around 50 percent greater than that of previous-production F-16s. 
How these aircraft can be utilized depends on the scenario. In the gray zone, fighters give Taipei a flexible means of visually identifying, shadowing, and escorting PLA aircraft, allowing it to demonstrate control and resolve without immediately escalating toward the use of surface-to-air weapons. The new Block 70s are also relevant because of the high tempo of Chinese military flights around Taiwan: Taipei believes Beijing is attempting to deplete the readiness of its air force with interception demands. New airframes help meet the operational tempo. 
They could also be valuable during a limited blockade, quarantine or coercive operation. By patrolling threatened air corridors, escorting aircraft, investigating contacts and contesting Chinese attempts to establish de facto control of the airspace around the island, the F-16s could give Taipei options for resisting coercion short of opening a broader air campaign. 
In the event of an all-out war, the ROCAF would serve as a complicating factor. Suppression of an opponent’s air operations is resource intensive: any surviving Taiwanese fighter force would require the PLA to continue allocating ISR, strike aircraft, missiles, and combat air patrols to finding, suppressing, and defending against it. Large-scale amphibious and airborne operations are particularly vulnerable to disruption and normally require the attacker to establish at least local and temporary control of the air and sea. Even a small surviving ROCAF fighter force would therefore be a threat the PLA could not safely ignore.
The new F-16s do not solve Taiwan’s wartime airpower problem, nor do they negate the need to invest in mobile and survivable asymmetric systems. Instead, they preserve Taiwanese airpower as a usable instrument across the spectrum from peacetime coercion to full-scale conflict. The strategic situation may have changed in the two decades since this purchase was first proposed, but they remain valuable assets.

articles.title: India’s Foreign Minister Jaishankar Openly Calls Out the US
articles.full_text:
Previously, India sorted out its differences with friendly nations quietly. Last week, it aired its grievance with Washington publicly.
India’s Minister of External Affairs Dr S. Jaishankar in a discussion with Daniel Russel, vice president for International Security and Diplomacy at Asia Society Policy Institute, New York, Sept. 29, 2026.
On September 28, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi had a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump to review progress in bilateral cooperation. In a post on X, Modi described the conversation as “productive.” “We reviewed our bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas. We agreed to maintain close engagement to take our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward,” he said.
While Modi’s post about his conversation with Trump was not negative, it was far less effusive than in the past, even bland. As Yashraj Sharma observed in an article in Al Jazeera, it was a “cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a ‘good friend’ in previous years.”
The Trump-Modi phone call came at a time when already fraying bilateral relations hit yet another difficult phase.
Ten days earlier, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) of 2026, which gives the U.S. president the authority to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. India, which is among the largest buyers of Russian energy, could potentially be impacted.
India-U.S. cooperation has deepened and widened over the past two decades. Despite “complexities,” ties were expected to grow under Trump; the outlook was upbeat.
However, Trump 2.0 has not been good for the partnership. Within weeks of the inauguration of Trump’s second presidential term, ties began unravelling not only over tariffs and immigration but also Washington’s cozying up to Pakistan on a raft of issues, including terrorism, an issue that Delhi is highly sensitive about.
India was among the countries that were hit the hardest by Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” announced last year. Adding insult to injury, India was then slapped with another 25 percent “punitive tariffs” for buying Russian oil.
Should the U.S. press ahead with imposing SRIA on India, it would hit India’s oil imports and, consequently, its energy security.
Over the past 19 months, although Indians took note of Trump’s abrasive remarks and insensitive tweets, they took it in their stride. The diplomatic establishment seemed to have adopted a patient wait-and-watch policy. India, after all, needed the U.S and benefited from economic and security cooperation with Washington. The current uncertainty was seen as temporary.
However, that mood in Delhi is changing. Its patience with Trump seems to be wearing thin. Officials and analysts are calling on the government to be more realistic in its assessment of the current India-U.S. relationship.
In an article in The Week, Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the U.S., wrote: “We need to accept, without caveats, that the relationship has cratered significantly. In America’s eyes, India is not the strategic partner that we believed we were.”
A change is evident not just in Delhi’s mood but also, in its approach.
“India has reached the end of its tether with Trump,” a former official in India’s MEA told The Diplomat. “In the past we abhorred megaphone diplomacy, preferring to sort out nettlesome issues with friends quietly and only via diplomatic channels. That was India’s approach towards Russia’s intervention in Afghanistan in 1979, and its invasion in Ukraine in 2022, for example. But that is clearly changing,” he said. “India today is not averse to calling out, even friends, on difficult matters if core concerns are being undermined.”
This change was on full display last week during India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar’s visit to the U.S.
At an event at the Asia Society in New York, Jaishankar did not hold back in drawing attention to Washington’s lack of “understanding or appreciation or empathy” for Delhi on issues of concern and sensitivity to the latter. He was referring to Washington’s courting of Pakistan despite the latter’s support for anti-India terrorism. “If one of my primary concerns is not fully appreciated by my partner, then clearly there is an impact of that on the relationship,” he said. Although he did not mention the U.S. by name, it was evident who he was referring to.
Strong India-U.S. relations have enjoyed bipartisan support in the U.S. over the past two decades. Whenever differences surfaced or ties frayed, Indian officials would avoid airing grievances to the media. They seemed willing to bide their time in the hope that this was a mere hiccup, a troubled phase that could be navigated. India being important to the U.S. in its strategy to contain a rising China, it was widely believed that the strategic partnership was solid.
But with the U.S.-China relationship seemingly moving to a phase of competitive coexistence rather than confrontation, India’s role in Washington’s containment strategy against China could decline. As Indian academic Atul Mishra pointed out, “If balancing China is no longer a priority, then India’s importance within America’s strategic calculus goes down.”
Especially after the recent meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, cracks are visible in the once-solid belief that India is important to the U.S. Apprehensions have deepened further amid Trump’s courting of Pakistan.
There are other reasons why the current troubled phase in India-U.S. ties may not be as temporary as Delhi believed over the past year. There is a growing perception that the fraying partnership may survive the end of Trump’s term.
According to Sarna, the current downturn in India-U.S. relations cannot be attributed to Trump alone. “Economic nationalism, racial supremacism, moral poverty, naked aggression and wanton disregard for international law and norms are trends which will outlast Trump; on many issues the centre has moved in American politics,” he argues, pointing out that Trump’s successor, be it U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio or even a Democrat politician, “may not be much different [from Trump], though a tad predictable.”
Meanwhile, all eyes in India have turned to India’s Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal’s ongoing visit to the U.S. Many rounds of talks have taken place so far, and while India and the U.S. reached a framework for an interim trade agreement in February 2026, a final Bilateral Trade Agreement remains elusive.
Ahead of his U.S. visit, Goyal said that the India-U.S. trade pact was “almost done and dusted.” Should the two sides firm up an agreement soon, that could lighten the gloomy mood in Delhi somewhat. Of course, much will depend on what the final agreement brings India.
An agreement that is heavily weighted against Indian interests can be expected to deepen the prevailing pessimism in Delhi over its ties with the U.S.

articles.title: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit
articles.full_text:
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.
It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.
However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia.
The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations. In 2024, the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Sino-Russian diplomatic relations and a year in which the pandemic was still fresh in mind and the war in Ukraine was very much ongoing, Russian President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to China in May and issued a joint statement. It included the following passage:
“China and Russia will continue to firmly defend the results of the victory of the Second World War and the postwar world order enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, and oppose the negation, distortion, and falsification of the history of World War II. They plan to solemnly celebrate the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Soviet Union’s Patriotic War in 2025 and jointly promote a correct view of the history of World War II.”
This statement signaled that China and Russia intended to jointly insist on what they view as the “correct history” of WWII to the world, while refusing to accept any historical perspective that differs from their own.
In March 2025, at a press conference on the occasion of China’s National People’s Congress, State Councilor Wang Yi stated that, marking the 80th anniversary of victory in WWII, China and Russia were reaffirming that they had fought together in Asia and Europe at the cost of blood, and went on to say that, building on this past, the two countries would jointly promote a correct understanding of WWII history, defend the fruits of that victory, uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core, and advance the international order in a more just and reasonable direction. China and Russia have thus pledged not only to reaffirm their wartime partnership but to jointly seek to shape the present international order on that basis. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.
Then, on May 9, 2025, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Russia and issued a joint statement with the Russian president. This statement explicitly identified Japanese militarism and Nazi Germany as the adversaries China and Russia fought in WWII, and made clear that China and Russia would together resist any moves to revive the militarism or Nazism of the past. On Japan specifically, the statement declared that “the Japanese government should learn lessons from the brutal crimes it committed in history, exercise caution in its words and deeds on historical issues such as the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely cut ties with militarism that once brought deep disasters to the peoples of the world and Japan itself.”
In its discourse on WWII, China was not only seeking to spread what it calls the “correct historical perspective” together with Russia, but was also issuing strong warnings against “Japanese militarism.” And this was positioned not merely as a matter of the past but — particularly in the context of the Sino-Russian relationship — as something linked to joint efforts toward a “just” reshaping of the international order.
In 2025, China made a qualitative leap in its narrative on history, in both substance and in method. China generated narratives connected to the invalidity of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, the Taiwan issue, and the status of Okinawa — areas directly linked to China’s interests in the First Island Chain. Yet China’s actions were moving faster than its words; its military activity had already extended well beyond the First Island Chain, expanding into the Second Island Chain, the Western Pacific, and the South Pacific.
From around the time of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November 2025 and into 2026, China’s verbal attacks on Japan began to employ the term “neo-militarism,” and its criticism of Japan became more comprehensive. Japan’s security policy as a whole began to be characterized and challenged as “neo-militarism.”
In May 2026, when Putin made another official visit to China and a Sino-Russian joint statement was issued, language criticizing Japan’s “neo-militarism” and “remilitarization” was incorporated into the text, which represented an expansion of Sino-Russian historical cooperation on WWII. China also sought to extend its criticism of Japan to countries beyond Russia, inserting language critical of Japan — such as opposition to “militarism” — into joint statements issued in the context of bilateral relationships with various countries. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026 as well, the Chinese representative strongly criticized Japan using terms such as “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov joined in, expressing agreement with the Chinese position by similarly characterizing Japan as following a path of militarism.

The United States and China were Allied nations in WWII. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.
Then, on May 9, 2025, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Russia and issued a joint statement with the Russian president. This statement explicitly identified Japanese militarism and Nazi Germany as the adversaries China and Russia fought in WWII, and made clear that China and Russia would together resist any moves to revive the militarism or Nazism of the past. On Japan specifically, the statement declared that “the Japanese government should learn lessons from the brutal crimes it committed in history, exercise caution in its words and deeds on historical issues such as the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely cut ties with militarism that once brought deep disasters to the peoples of the world and Japan itself.”
In its discourse on WWII, China was not only seeking to spread what it calls the “correct historical perspective” together with Russia, but was also issuing strong warnings against “Japanese militarism.” And this was positioned not merely as a matter of the past but — particularly in the context of the Sino-Russian relationship — as something linked to joint efforts toward a “just” reshaping of the international order.
In 2025, China made a qualitative leap in its narrative on history, in both substance and in method. China generated narratives connected to the invalidity of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, the Taiwan issue, and the status of Okinawa — areas directly linked to China’s interests in the First Island Chain. Yet China’s actions were moving faster than its words; its military activity had already extended well beyond the First Island Chain, expanding into the Second Island Chain, the Western Pacific, and the South Pacific.
From around the time of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November 2025 and into 2026, China’s verbal attacks on Japan began to employ the term “neo-militarism,” and its criticism of Japan became more comprehensive. Japan’s security policy as a whole began to be characterized and challenged as “neo-militarism.”
In May 2026, when Putin made another official visit to China and a Sino-Russian joint statement was issued, language criticizing Japan’s “neo-militarism” and “remilitarization” was incorporated into the text, which represented an expansion of Sino-Russian historical cooperation on WWII. China also sought to extend its criticism of Japan to countries beyond Russia, inserting language critical of Japan — such as opposition to “militarism” — into joint statements issued in the context of bilateral relationships with various countries. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026 as well, the Chinese representative strongly criticized Japan using terms such as “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov joined in, expressing agreement with the Chinese position by similarly characterizing Japan as following a path of militarism.
Which brings us to the recent U.S.-China summit, where Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump raised the subject of the wartime relationship between the United States and China in WWII. The United States and China were Allied nations in WWII. But in light of the account above, China’s recent discourse on WWII is certainly not limited to pointing out historical facts or evoking memories of the past. And for Japan, that is cause for concern.
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.
It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.
KAWASHIMA Shin is a professor at the University of Tokyo.
articles.summary: How China is weaponizing WWII history

articles.title: Philippines Rejects Chinese Claim to ‘Sovereign Rights’ Over Waters Around Batanes
articles.full_text:
The Chinese activities around the Philippines’ northernmost province represent the opening of a new front in the maritime struggle between the two nations.
A screenshot from a video released by the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) shows a rigid-hulled inflatable boat from PCG circling the Jia Ha Ke 7, a Chinese research vessel, in the waters off Batanes, Philippines, Oct. 1, 2026.
The Philippine government today rejected China’s assertion that it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over waters off Batanes, the country’s northernmost province, a day after the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove away a Chinese research vessel operating in the area.
The PCG said yesterday that it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge the Jia Ha Ke 7, a Chinese research ship, that had been “loitering” around 37 nautical miles northwest of Batanes for the past four days. During the confrontation, PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said that a China Coast Guard vessel also moved in and “repeatedly tried to shield the research vessel and block the PCG ship.”
The Philippine operation nonetheless “successfully disrupted the unauthorized marine scientific research” being conducted by the Jia He Ke 7 and “compelled it to leave the position it had held off Itbayat, Batanes, for four days.”
China’s embassy in Manila responded by claiming that the Chinese research vessel was “conducting normal operations in waters under China’s jurisdiction in accordance with international law.” It urged the Philippines to “genuinely respect China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the relevant waters,” and to cease its “provocative interference with China’s normal scientific research activities.”
In a statement today, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said it “firmly and strongly rejects” the Chinese claims of sovereignty over the waters around Batanes, a group of islands lying midway between Taiwan and the Philippines’ Luzon island. It argued that the Chinese research vessel was operating well within the country’s 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), where, according to the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), marine scientific research can only be conducted “with the consent of the coastal State.”
The Chinese activities around Batanes represent the opening of a new front in the maritime struggle between Beijing and Manila, which has manifested at different features in the South China Sea, particularly at Scarborough Shoal and at various parts of the Spratly Islands.
In late June, at a symposium at Jinan University in Guangzhou, Chinese scholars from several institutions argued that China enjoyed sovereignty over Batanes. According to a report by Jinan University, which was later published by the Guangdong-based news outlet Newsgd, participants described the Batanes Islands as a “natural geographical extension” of Taiwan, and said that they therefore belonged to China.
Philippine Defense Minister Gilberto Teodoro subsequently dismissed the claims, describing them as “baseless” and “ludicrous.” “So this is concerning, and it is something that must be challenged,” he added.
This week’s events seem to validate the warnings of observers who said at the time that the scholars’ remarks might open the way to official claims by Beijing. Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, argued that the claims about Batanes were little more than the “territorial wet dreams” of Beijing-aligned scholars, but that such ideas “could potentially seep into official discourse if they fit ethno-nationalist agendas.”
While Manila does not view its South China Sea possessions any differently from its “home islands” – it considers all to be inalienable parts of the Philippines – it has reason to be  concerned about this latest development. Batanes is both the smallest and least populated of the Philippines’ 82 provinces, and is home to 18,937 people, as per the 2024 Philippine census. This nonetheless compares to just 406 for the Kalayaan Island Group, as Manila refers to its nine occupied features in the Spratlys.
The extension of Chinese gray zone tactics to “core” Philippine islands over which Manila’s sovereignty has never seriously been challenged could mark a considerable escalation of the maritime dispute between the two nations.

articles.title: Indonesia Needs to Do More to Tackle the Region’s Transboundary Haze Problem
articles.full_text:
Under Prabowo Subianto, leadership on the issue has been lacking – and tens of millions are suffering as a result.
Air pollution in North Kayong regency, West Kalimantan province, Indonesia, Sep. 27, 2026.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto is the key leader in ASEAN who can and should do better in haze management in the coming years. The current haze situation affecting Southeast Asia is, to a certain extent, a reflection of his leadership and management, given that most of it stems from fires happening in his country.
Forests and peatlands in Indonesia have been burning substantially this year and millions of people in Southeast Asia are suffering as a result. In early September, Kuching had the worst air quality of any large city on earth. Malaysian authorities declared a state of emergency in the Serian district of Sarawak, as the Air Pollutant Index exceeded 500. The Philippines closed schools throughout Metro Manila and more than 12 provinces. The regional haze monitor in ASEAN reached level three, the most severe on the scale.
Indonesia needs to improve its leadership on the haze management issue.
Fire has been used to clear land as it is cheaper than alternative methods. Plantations, companies, and farmers burn the vegetation before the planting season, instead of paying for mechanical clearing. The drained peatlands of Sumatra and Kalimantan also get burnt and this adds fuel to the fire. These fires continue for weeks and release even more toxic particles than an ordinary forest fire. Due to the current El Niño climate cycle, there are drier and longer dry seasons, worsening the situation, as experienced in 1997, 2015, and 2019.
The solutions are relatively straightforward. They are to rewet the drained peatland, enforce a moratorium on new plantation permits in forest and peat areas, punish the recalcitrant companies, and publicize their names so they can be held responsible.
Importantly, there needs to be close tracking of fires and smallholder burning, as well as enhanced local fire-response capacity so as to minimize, control, and extinguish fires before they get out of control. Satellite technology can be used to facilitate the tracking too. These pre-emptive and preventive measures, in addition to effective firefighting capabilities, need to be in place to address this haze situation effectively.
There is precedent for effective action. In 2015, during his first term in office, President Joko Widodo encountered the disastrous 2015 fires, during which 2.6 million hectares were burned and more than a hundred million lives were affected. He created the Peatland Restoration Agency that rewetted more than a million hectares of degraded peat. He also set up a standing haze task force. Furthermore, in 2019, he put a permanent moratorium on new peatlands and primary forest permits.
The results were positive. The fires decreased subsequently. For instance, significant fires in 2023 burned about 1.6 million hectares, a decrease of a million acres compared to 2015. Towards the end of Jokowi’s term in 2024, the Ministry of Environment and Forestry reported a 59.4 percent year-on-year drop in hotspots.
This year, President Prabowo visited fire-hit provinces in Sumatra and Kalimantan. He deployed police and military staff on the ground, and in addition to police investigations, he pledged to revoke the permits of guilty companies. However, these efforts may be inadequate. The cumulative hotspots in late July 2026 exceeded the dreadful 2019 numbers. More needs to be done to anticipate and prevent the wildfire problem.
Other than naming the responsible corporations and holding them accountable, there should be the public prosecution of the indicted corporate leaders, open publication of the concession-ownership data and increased resources for peatland wetting, along with enhanced fire-fighting capabilities.
The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, signed in 2002, will only work when the Prabowo administration intentionally and effectively implements the full range of effective, preventive, punitive and responsive measures. Prabowo and his government can implement a combination of measures for the well-being of their citizens and the neighboring countries.
Along with the hundreds of millions in Southeast Asia affected by the haze, we share the hope that the Indonesian administration can be more effective and efficient in managing and reducing the causes of the haze problem, which has plagued Southeast Asia over the past month, so that we can all benefit from cleaner, haze-free air again.

articles.title: A Tajik Bank Shuts Side Door for Russian Cardholders
articles.full_text:
Humo Bank’s ultimatum to its Russian clients shows how Western sanctions can shape Tajikistan’s banking sector.
Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline.
The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year.
With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles.
Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company, the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe. An investigation by The Bell found last year that Sberbank clients could send money to Revolut and N26 accounts through Central Asian intermediaries, with the funds appearing to originate from Dushanbe or Tashkent.
The Humo ultimatum follows a year of Western pressure on Tajik banks. In October 2025, the European Union included Dushanbe City Bank, Spitamen, and Commercebank of Tajikistan in its 19th sanctions package, targeting banks closely linked to Russia’s financial system or processing cross-border payments that support the Russian economy. The three banks held roughly a fifth of all deposits in Tajikistan, and other Tajik banks responded by restricting transfers to Russia. In December, Revolut stopped accepting top-ups from cards issued in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, citing payment systems’ classification of those countries as high-risk. The EU removed the three Tajik banks from its sanctions list in April 2026, with the National Bank crediting improved compliance and anti-money laundering standards.
For Dushanbe, the stakes go well beyond fees collected from Russian cardholders. Remittances, mostly from Tajik migrants in Russia, reached $5.8 billion in 2024, or the equivalent of 45.3 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP, the highest share in the world. By the end of 2024, over 90 percent of payments in Tajik-Russian trade were settled in rubles, and the head of the National Bank said Tajik banks work only with Russian banks not under sanctions. Tajikistan needs its financial channels to Russia open and its banks connected to SWIFT and Visa at the same time.
Neither Humo nor the National Bank has said whether the decision came from regulators, payment systems, or the bank’s own risk assessment. But a young bank that watched three of its peers cut off from European counterparties has every reason to shed remotely onboarded Russian clients before Brussels or Visa forces its hand. Russians will likely take their business to Kyrgyz and Uzbek banks, as they did when Kazakhstan closed its doors, until those banks face the same pressure.

articles.title: Trouble in Shangri-La? Why Bruneians Are Going to Australia for Illegal Migrant Work
articles.full_text:
Unemployed Bruneians are using Australian tourist visas to work as fruit pickers.
A Royal Brunei Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner in Melbourne, Australia, Feb. 22, 2024.
To the outside world, Brunei, the tiny Southeast Asian monarchy, looks like a Shangri-La. The country, with a population of less than half a million, has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita in the world. Its benevolent Sultan has ensured free healthcare and education and highly subsidized food and housing for his subjects.
There is no income tax. Brunei has the highest per capita car ownership in ASEAN – an average of two cars per household – and a high prevalence of foreign domestic workers, locally called “amah,” predominantly hailing from Indonesia and the Philippines.
Given this background, the news of educated Bruneians going to Australia to work illegally on agricultural farms as fruit-pickers was shocking for someone who has worked in Brunei for 10 years.
But a Reddit discussion on Brunei unemployment revealed that something is amiss in the Sultanate. Many unemployed people blamed foreign workers for taking their jobs in the private sector.
For some, the easiest way out was Australia. The Bruneian passport, ranked 19th in the world, opens visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to 163 countries.
The Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) gives a three-month tourist visa for just A$20. Although it is illegal for ETA holders to work, and if caught, the visa can be cancelled, for some desperate Bruneians the risk is worth taking, as A$30-A$50 per hour looks pretty good even after taking travel, board, and lodging into consideration.
Although Australia has a program called the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) scheme, also called backpacker visa, which allows travelers to work during their stay to help finance their holiday, it comes with several caveats. There is generally a six-month limit on working for the same employer. More importantly, the scheme is available only to citizens of more than 40 partner countries and Brunei is not among them. This may explain why some Bruneians are using the ETA as a backdoor route to Australia in search of farm work.
How has the situation come to this pass? One cannot find obvious signs of poverty in Brunei, unlike in many Southeast Asian countries. I have never seen a Bruneian begging on the streets.
The problem is that educated youth are not finding employment in one of the richest countries in the world. It sounds paradoxical. Even more ironic is the fact that the hydrocarbon sector, which brought so much wealth to the country, is also contributing to unemployment. The Dutch Disease is at work in Brunei. When 90 percent of export revenues come from oil and gas, it can stunt the growth of other sectors such as agriculture, tourism, and industry.
A communications consultant, who asked not to be named, said: “The economy is just broken and is too skewed in one direction. Too much emphasis on the hydrocarbon sector has not only shrunk the job market but also made different clusters of the economy stagnant.” She added: “Outside of oil and gas, what do we have? What job opportunities are there?”
Brunei’s 2025 Labor Force Survey, published in July using the International Labor Organization reference population aged 15 and above, showed unemployment rising to 11,800 people, or 5.1 percent, from 4.8 percent in 2024. Brunei’s national headline measure, covering those aged 18 and above, was 5.0 percent. 
Youth unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 stood at 18.4 percent. The gap by sex was stark: 15.3 percent for young men and 23.7 percent for young women. This means nearly one in four young women in the labor force who were seeking work did not find it. 
Time-related underemployment rose from 15,600 to 19,500 people. These were workers who wanted additional hours, worked fewer than 40 hours, and were available for more work.
The important highlight of the survey is that median monthly income from employment fell from BN$1,000 in 2024 to BN$950 in 2025. 
Siti Fatimahwati Pehin Dato Musa and Pg Dr Siti Rozaidah Pg Hj Idris of Universiti Brunei Darussalam, in their seminal 2022 work, “Addressing Issues of Unemployment in Brunei: The Mismatch Between Employers’ Expectations and Employees’ Aspirations,” wrote that the majority of young people seek prestigious jobs and that there seems to be a risk-averse attitude among them. Most young people aspire to jobs that are in the professional, managerial, or technical sectors.
This preference for secure jobs is also reflected in Brunei’s employment structure. The government is the biggest employer in Brunei, and it is the most sought-after avenue for any young Bruneian because of lifelong financial security.
The 2022 study found that the mindset of relying on government jobs was responsible for a lower preference for jobs in the private sector and other sectors. Another factor highlighted by the study was that most Bruneians are averse to manual work.
A social media consultant said that in the good old days, when oil was hitting more than $140 per barrel, everything was humming along. He said the only way out of the current economic trap is diversification. Brunei should learn from Gulf countries, which have reduced their dependence on the oil and gas sector. Even a country like Saudi Arabia has started diversifying its economy, he pointed out.
“The notion that Brunei is a utopia that is shielded from turbulent economic and natural forces no longer exists today,” he added.
Discussion of agricultural work in Australia has been doing the rounds on Brunei’s social media. Australia is entering its harvest season, when farmers face a perennial shortage of seasonal labor. WHM travelers are an important source of this workforce and can legally take jobs such as fruit picking. But Bruneians are not eligible for the WHM scheme, and working on an ETA remains illegal.
The Australian High Commission in Bandar Seri Begawan has a dedicated page on its website warning Bruneians against visa scams and making clear that an ETA does not permit them to work in Australia.
Although the Bruneian dollar is stronger than the Australian dollar because of Brunei’s currency interchangeability agreement with the Singapore dollar, for an unemployed young Bruneian A$30-A$50 an hour is worth taking risk. According to wage.is, the minimum wage in Brunei is BN$2.62/hr (A$2.88) as of 2026. The average gross monthly salary is BN$2,500 (A$2,752); the same amount could be earned in just about two weeks of fruit picking in Australia. 
This is the reason why some of Brunei’s educated young people are now leaving home to do agricultural labor in Australia.
A teacher at Universiti Brunei Darussalam pointed out the paradox: “The reason why we have so many foreign workers doing manual jobs, even in the agriculture sector, is that many times we are told that Bruneians are averse to manual work. Here, a young Bruneian, leaving the comforts of home, is ready to go to Australia to do manual work on farms. I am not sure about the monetary benefit if you take into account air tickets, board, and lodging.”
Is it a case of the grass looking greener on the other side of the fence? Or are young Bruneians simply trying to make a quick buck while waiting for their chance in the long queue of the unemployed? It might be both.
To the outside world, Brunei, the tiny Southeast Asian monarchy, looks like a Shangri-La. The country, with a population of less than half a million, has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita in the world. Its benevolent Sultan has ensured free healthcare and education and highly subsidized food and housing for his subjects.
There is no income tax. Brunei has the highest per capita car ownership in ASEAN – an average of two cars per household – and a high prevalence of foreign domestic workers, locally called “amah,” predominantly hailing from Indonesia and the Philippines.
Given this background, the news of educated Bruneians going to Australia to work illegally on agricultural farms as fruit-pickers was shocking for someone who has worked in Brunei for 10 years.
articles.summary: Unemployed Bruneians are using Australian tourist visas to work as fruit pickers.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Local Elections Are Not About China, President Lai, or the United States
articles.full_text:
Candidates across Taiwan are campaigning on local issues that vary by city – not topics like cross-strait relations. What can we learn from these elections?
Legislator and New Taipei City mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui and New Taipei City councilor Chang Chin-hao at the opening of their joint campaign headquarters in Xizhi District, New Taipei, Taiwan, Sep. 28, 2026.
This November, Taiwanese voters go to the polls to elect mayors, city councilors, and village chiefs. Many foreign policy observers will read the results as a verdict on Taiwanese attitudes toward China, President Lai Ching-te, Trump, or a potential war. That would be an analytical mistake. The outcomes cannot be explained by how voters feel about independence, unification, China, the United States, or any other national issue. As the saying goes, local elections are about local issues.
Decades of data show that Taiwanese voters prioritize China, sovereignty, and Taiwan’s future in national elections, but we have little longitudinal data on how they decide in local ones. What we do know is that voters often cast ballots for mayor or city council differently than they do for president. For example, Taichung and New Taipei have elected a Kuomintang (KMT) mayor in each of the last two local elections, yet a majority of their voters still supported Lai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in 2024. Electing a mayor from one party hardly means a city will back that party’s presidential candidate.
Candidates across Taiwan are campaigning on local issues that vary by city, such as housing, public transportation, and urban renewal. Some touch on national issues, but most mayoral and city council candidates avoid them, since talking about national issues or polarizing figures could cost them votes. 
One telling example is the absence of both the DPP and KMT party leaders from most mayoral and city council election campaign advertisements. Lai, who is also the DPP chair, and KMT chair Cheng Li-wun are both deeply polarizing figures, specifically for their positions on national issues including China and Taiwan’s relationship with the United States. Featuring Lai or Cheng in a local campaign invites voters to see local candidates as extensions of their party’s divisive leadership rather than a local candidate. In Taichung, for example, former president Tsai Ing-wen can be found far more frequently in DPP campaign ads than Lai.
Regardless of which party does well, both will likely frame the results as a sign that Taiwanese civil society broadly supports their policies, including on cross-strait politics. It would again be a mistake to buy that message. Local election results are not a referendum on party support or on attitudes toward the party chairs. During Tsai’s presidency, for instance, the DPP performed dismally in both sets of local elections, yet won clear victories in the national elections that followed. In Taiwan, national and local elections are neither tied to nor predictive of each other.
So what can we learn from these elections? Most importantly, they will set the chess pieces for 2028. A few key races will show which parties gain confidence and may shift factional politics.
One key example is New Taipei City, traditionally a KMT stronghold, and arguably the most important race this cycle. Outgoing mayor Hou Yu-ih is leaving office with high approval ratings despite his failed 2024 presidential campaign. His replacement should have an easy race, but the KMT candidate, Lee Shu-chuan, is struggling. Although he has a history of being a strong bureaucrat, Lee has run a lackluster campaign and lacks charisma. So far, his campaign has been bland. 
His DPP opponent, Su Chiao-hui, is performing strongly for a DPP candidate in New Taipei. As the daughter of DPP heavyweight and former New Taipei mayor Su Tseng-chang, she is both a family legacy and a demonstration of long commitment to the city. She has cleverly avoided national discourse, emphasizing instead her record of delivering for her community. 
Su’s campaign is leaving a far stronger impression among New Taipei voters than many suspected she would. The race is very close, and a DPP victory would dent KMT confidence heading into 2028 because New Taipei was supposed to be an easy KMT victory.
Importantly, a Su victory would not necessarily be a victory for Lai. Su is not a member of Lai’s faction, and although her win would be a major boost for the party, it would not raise Lai’s standing within it. Her victory would, however, help the DPP campaign with strong leadership in 2028. It would also send a message to the KMT that their traditional voter strongholds need more from their candidates than just a strong bureaucratic record.
Another example is the increasingly contentious Taipei race between the DPP’s Puma Shen and the KMT’s Chiang Wan-an. Chiang, the incumbent mayor and a 2028 presidential hopeful, was expected to win re-election easily, but Shen is running a strong campaign. Though best known as the founder of the disinformation research organization Doublethink Lab and the civil defense organization Kuma Academy, Shen has focused not on national topics like civil defense, but on improving Taipei’s livability. Chiang, meanwhile, has faced more scandals this campaign than in the rest of his tenure, and has so far run a particularly lackluster campaign. He is still expected to win, but Shen’s showing is unexpectedly competitive.
To a degree, the Taipei race is less about who wins, and more about whether Chiang can build momentum for a 2028 presidential run. If Chiang wins by only a few percentage points, it would be a big victory for the DPP and would hurt Chiang’s momentum if he hopes to become the KMT’s 2028 nominee. Even if Shen loses, his performance has been strong enough that he likely has a political future in the DPP. 
Though unlikely, if the DPP were unexpectedly successful in taking both Taipei and New Taipei, this would probably lead to a political narrative about the KMT losing its traditional territory in northern Taiwan – not dissimilar to the narrative that emerged in 2018 after Han Kuo-yu of the KMT unexpectedly captured the mayorship of Kaohsiung, a long-time DPP stronghold. It should not, however, be over-interpreted to infer a permanent change in Taiwan civil society or a reflection of national attitudes. If Taipei and New Taipei elect DPP mayors, it will be due to the KMT mismanaging their candidates and campaigns, combined with smart, effective campaigning from Su and Shen.
Even if Chiang wins, the KMT faces a difficult presidential primary season. The field is already crowded: outgoing Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen, Legislative Yuan president Han Kuo-yu, and KMT chair Cheng Li-wun are all contending for the nomination. Cheng herself faces a difficult future if the KMT does poorly. Though she is not on the ballot, her opponents within the party are likely to push her to resign, which would leave the KMT’s 2028 presidential leadership up in the air.

While the “Blue-White Alliance” has been a steadfast partnership thus far during Lai’s first term, the outward show of friendship has buckled this cycle. articles.title: Japan and Australia: Toward a More Autonomous and Resilient Partnership
articles.full_text:
As Washington’s reliability wavers, Tokyo and Canberra are learning to depend on each other.
Japan’s Defense Minister Nakatani Gen, right, and Australia’s Defense Minister Richard Marles held a joint press announcement aboard the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force’s Mogami-class stealth frigate JS Mikuma at the Japanese naval base in Yokosuka, Japan, on Sept. 5, 2025.
The security environment in the Indo-Pacific is undergoing a profound transformation. Cooperation among revisionist powers, including China, Russia, and North Korea, is deepening, while the strategic priorities of the United States — the country that has long underpinned the regional order — are also changing. At the same time, technological advances in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, unmanned platforms, quantum technologies, and cyber capabilities are fundamentally changing the character of warfare and the sources of military advantage.
Against this backdrop, Japan and Australia have deepened their comprehensive security partnership across military and economic domains. What matters increasingly is their ability to build both strategic autonomy and strategic resilience.
Strategic autonomy does not mean “independence” from the United States. Rather, it means reducing excessive dependence on any single major power and preserving greater room for strategic choice and freedom of action. Strategic resilience, meanwhile, refers to the ability to withstand and recover from strategic shocks, whether they take the form of military conflict, economic coercion, supply-chain disruption, or energy crises. Together, these two concepts provide a useful framework for thinking about the current state and future direction of Japan–Australia cooperation.
For much of the post-Cold War period, both Japan and Australia benefited from what might be called “dual dependence.” In security terms, both relied heavily on the United States, while economically they developed increasingly deep interdependence with China. This arrangement allowed them to enjoy security at relatively low defense costs while benefiting substantially from China’s economic growth.
As U.S.–China rivalry and broader great-power competition intensify, however, this model is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet neither replacing dependence on the United States with dependence on China, nor pursuing economic decoupling from China, is a viable option for either country. Rather, the goal is to diversify dependence itself — to expand the range of partners and capabilities available so that neither country becomes excessively vulnerable to the decisions of any single major power.
This is the direction the Japan–Australia relationship has taken over the past few years. While maintaining their respective alliances with the United States, Japan and Australia have strengthened their own capabilities and built a more autonomous bilateral security relationship — one that goes beyond simply “supplementing” the U.S. military presence in the region.
The cooperation surrounding the Australian Navy’s acquisition of Japanese-designed Mogami-class frigates is a good example. Its significance extends well beyond the transfer of a particular platform. Developed into sustained cooperation across joint development, production, maintenance, and future technologies, it could strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries — enhancing their ability not just to acquire military capabilities but to produce, maintain, and sustain them over time.
Australia’s strategic depth is equally important. Japan is geographically located on the front line of the First Island Chain, whereas Australia can provide vast training areas as well as logistics, maintenance, and rear-area support. By developing these arrangements during peacetime, the two countries can build the capacity to sustain military operations over a prolonged period in the event of a crisis or conflict. This will also become increasingly important as the operational horizon of the Japan Self-Defense Forces expands beyond the First Island Chain toward the wider Pacific.
The same logic applies to economic security. Building more diversified supply chains for energy, critical minerals, critical technologies, and other strategic goods can enhance the autonomy and resilience of both Japan and Australia. Importantly, however, such efforts are not limited to the bilateral relationship.
One example is a regional initiative such as “POWERR Asia.” Through mechanisms for energy stockpiling, sharing, and emergency supply arrangements, Japan and Australia could help strengthen energy resilience across the wider Indo-Pacific. The objective would be to create regional networks capable of absorbing shocks rather than leaving individual countries vulnerable to sudden disruptions or external pressure.
A similar logic should guide engagement with Pacific Island countries. Assistance to these countries should not be viewed solely through the prism of strategic competition with China; instead, Japan and Australia have focused on strengthening resilience in areas such as infrastructure, energy, communications, and economic security. The aim should be to create an environment in which smaller states are not forced to “choose” between the United States and China simply because they lack viable alternatives.
Ultimately, this strategy is neither about achieving “independence” from the United States nor about “containing” China. The U.S. military presence will remain indispensable to regional stability, while economic and diplomatic relations with China will continue to matter greatly. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate dependence, which is neither possible nor desirable, but to diversify it in ways that preserve greater freedom of action.
This logic should eventually be extended to the region as a whole. By building networks through which regional countries complement one another’s capabilities across defense, energy, technology, infrastructure, and economic security, the Indo-Pacific can become more resilient to strategic shocks and less vulnerable to sudden changes in the policies or preferences of major powers.
The ultimate purpose of Japan–Australia cooperation, therefore, extends beyond conventional alliance management or burden-sharing with the United States. It should contribute to building a region in which countries of the Indo-Pacific possess greater agency and a greater capacity to sustain stability and order.
In this sense, Japan–Australia cooperation should evolve from a partnership designed primarily to adapt to an order dominated by great powers into one that enables regional countries to play a greater role in shaping the regional order themselves.

articles.title: Time for ASEAN to Revive its Customs Union Vision
articles.full_text:
An idea rejected in 1986 deserves a second look.
As tariffs once again become bargaining tools for major powers, one of ASEAN’s key weaknesses is the fragmentation of its market across national tariff regimes. The revival of the Common External Tariff (CET) proposal, rejected four decades ago, raises a fundamental question: can ASEAN move beyond a mere “collection of assembly hubs” to become a higher-value-added economic region and a negotiating actor in its own right?
A Customs Union Proposal Rejected 40 Years Ago
ASEAN’s economic integration has been built on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), agreed in 1992 and implemented through the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme from 1993. The CEPT lowered intra-ASEAN tariffs on goods originating in the region. A CET, by contrast, would require member states to apply a common external tariff schedule to imports from outside ASEAN. Its adoption would take ASEAN beyond a free trade area and towards a customs union.
The CET is not a new idea. In August 1986, exactly 40 years ago, the Philippines, then ASEAN chair, proposed a customs union at the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting. The proposal called for intra-regional tariffs to be reduced gradually within a fixed time frame and for a common tariff to be imposed on imports from outside ASEAN. No consensus emerged: Indonesia opposed the deadline, while Singapore objected that the proposal could result in higher external tariffs. Intra-ASEAN trade then accounted for only about 20 percent of member states’ total trade, and their heavy dependence on external markets made a CET difficult to accept.
AFTA’s Success—and the Borders That Remain
ASEAN instead chose AFTA. This flexible form of integration eliminated most intra-regional tariffs while preserving each member state’s discretion over external tariffs. It supported ASEAN’s model of open regionalism – welcoming foreign investment and imported intermediate inputs while producing for global markets – and helped expand regional production networks. Yet many member states remained concentrated in assembly operations and dependent on external suppliers for key components, advanced materials and research and development. As a result, the value added retained within ASEAN did not rise commensurately with the value of its exports.
Under a fully functioning customs union, goods imported from outside the region could, after paying the common external tariff upon entering ASEAN, circulate freely within the bloc in principle. Certificates of origin and customs clearance procedures currently required for preferential intra-ASEAN trade would, in principle, no longer be necessary. With national tariff borders and rules of origin removed, companies could source the most suitable mix of parts and materials from across ASEAN and allocate production stages accordingly. Lower border costs would encourage intra-regional sourcing, the consolidation of production, and investment in higher-value activities.
Yet the flexibility that was once ASEAN’s strength is becoming a weakness amid intensifying geoeconomic competition. As tariffs, export controls, subsidies, and scrutiny of circumvention become increasingly intertwined with economic security, individual ASEAN members risk accepting different terms in separate negotiations with major powers. If this continues, companies may find it increasingly difficult to treat ASEAN as a single production base. More importantly, if member states continue to bargain separately on critical trade issues, not only regional supply chains but ASEAN centrality itself could be hollowed out.
A CET as a Platform for an Industrial Upgrade
In response to these concerns, the ASEAN Geoeconomics Report 2025 recommended that ASEAN pursue a CET alongside a compatible regional industrial policy. A common tariff alone, however, will not deliver an industrial upgrade; it must be combined with policies that connect the complementary strengths of member states and promote technology adoption, skills development, R&D and intra-regional sourcing. Only then can ASEAN retain more value added and create more high-quality jobs within the region. A CET alone is not sufficient, but it can provide the market foundation for such upgrading.
Realizing this vision will not be easy. ASEAN would have to agree on the treatment of customs revenue, trade-remedy measures and negotiating authority vis-à-vis third countries. It would also have to reconcile the FTAs concluded separately by individual member states. Existing agreements would need either to be consolidated into ASEAN-wide trade agreements or to have their preferential tariff rates and rules of origin harmonized across trading partners and product categories. If national tariff differentials remained, ASEAN would still need origin checks and the collection of tariff differences at internal borders to prevent imports from being diverted through lower-tariff members. The result would fall short of a full customs union.
Even so, ASEAN should not bury the idea once again. As a first step, member states should harmonize tariffs at low levels on critical inputs that cannot be adequately sourced within the region, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and critical minerals. This would not constitute a customs union, but would provide a practical test of whether a transition towards a CET is workable. In parallel, ASEAN should more closely integrate customs procedures, standards and conformity assessment, investment policy, skills development and R&D support. A Customs Union Proposal Rejected 40 Years Ago
ASEAN’s economic integration has been built on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), agreed in 1992 and implemented through the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme from 1993. The CEPT lowered intra-ASEAN tariffs on goods originating in the region. A CET, by contrast, would require member states to apply a common external tariff schedule to imports from outside ASEAN. Its adoption would take ASEAN beyond a free trade area and towards a customs union.
The CET is not a new idea. In August 1986, exactly 40 years ago, the Philippines, then ASEAN chair, proposed a customs union at the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting. The proposal called for intra-regional tariffs to be reduced gradually within a fixed time frame and for a common tariff to be imposed on imports from outside ASEAN. No consensus emerged: Indonesia opposed the deadline, while Singapore objected that the proposal could result in higher external tariffs. Intra-ASEAN trade then accounted for only about 20 percent of member states’ total trade, and their heavy dependence on external markets made a CET difficult to accept.
AFTA’s Success—and the Borders That Remain
ASEAN instead chose AFTA. This flexible form of integration eliminated most intra-regional tariffs while preserving each member state’s discretion over external tariffs. It supported ASEAN’s model of open regionalism – welcoming foreign investment and imported intermediate inputs while producing for global markets – and helped expand regional production networks. Yet many member states remained concentrated in assembly operations and dependent on external suppliers for key components, advanced materials and research and development. As a result, the value added retained within ASEAN did not rise commensurately with the value of its exports.
Under a fully functioning customs union, goods imported from outside the region could, after paying the common external tariff upon entering ASEAN, circulate freely within the bloc in principle. Certificates of origin and customs clearance procedures currently required for preferential intra-ASEAN trade would, in principle, no longer be necessary. With national tariff borders and rules of origin removed, companies could source the most suitable mix of parts and materials from across ASEAN and allocate production stages accordingly. Lower border costs would encourage intra-regional sourcing, the consolidation of production, and investment in higher-value activities.
Yet the flexibility that was once ASEAN’s strength is becoming a weakness amid intensifying geoeconomic competition. As tariffs, export controls, subsidies, and scrutiny of circumvention become increasingly intertwined with economic security, individual ASEAN members risk accepting different terms in separate negotiations with major powers. If this continues, companies may find it increasingly difficult to treat ASEAN as a single production base. More importantly, if member states continue to bargain separately on critical trade issues, not only regional supply chains but ASEAN centrality itself could be hollowed out.
A CET as a Platform for an Industrial Upgrade
In response to these concerns, the ASEAN Geoeconomics Report 2025 recommended that ASEAN pursue a CET alongside a compatible regional industrial policy. A common tariff alone, however, will not deliver an industrial upgrade; it must be combined with policies that connect the complementary strengths of member states and promote technology adoption, skills development, R&D and intra-regional sourcing. Only then can ASEAN retain more value added and create more high-quality jobs within the region. A CET alone is not sufficient, but it can provide the market foundation for such upgrading.
Realizing this vision will not be easy. ASEAN would have to agree on the treatment of customs revenue, trade-remedy measures and negotiating authority vis-à-vis third countries. It would also have to reconcile the FTAs concluded separately by individual member states. Existing agreements would need either to be consolidated into ASEAN-wide trade agreements or to have their preferential tariff rates and rules of origin harmonized across trading partners and product categories. If national tariff differentials remained, ASEAN would still need origin checks and the collection of tariff differences at internal borders to prevent imports from being diverted through lower-tariff members. The result would fall short of a full customs union.
Even so, ASEAN should not bury the idea once again. As a first step, member states should harmonize tariffs at low levels on critical inputs that cannot be adequately sourced within the region, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and critical minerals. This would not constitute a customs union, but would provide a practical test of whether a transition towards a CET is workable. In parallel, ASEAN should more closely integrate customs procedures, standards and conformity assessment, investment policy, skills development and R&D support. The objective should be to build a regional industrial base linking components and materials with more advanced stages of production.
ASEAN should aim for a customs union that preserves openness to critical inputs, reduces fragmentation within its regional market and encourages companies to invest on an ASEAN-wide basis. It should not become a “tariff fortress” that erects high barriers against the rest of the world. Rather, it should provide the institutional foundation for transforming ASEAN from a “collection of assembly hubs” dependent on cheap labor into an integrated economic region that builds deeper capabilities in technology, components and R&D—and retains more value added at home.
