articles.title: Russia’s Navy Shows Its Reach Around Japan’s Southwestern Islands
articles.full_text:
Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to a northern territory claimed by Japan comes amid a steady uptick in Russian naval activity near Japan’s southernmost islands.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visits the Yasny fish processing complex on Iturup island, Aug. 13, 2026.
President Vladimir Putin’s mid-August visit to the Kuril Islands, his first as Russia’s leader, inflamed a decades-old territorial dispute with Japan and drew worldwide attention to the two countries’ border in the northern Pacific. But over the past several years, Russian forces have been increasingly active far to the south, around Japan’s southwestern-most islands, in a demonstration of the Russian military’s reach and its willingness to challenge its rivals on its own and alongside China.
The dispute centers on the southernmost islands in the Kuril chain, which Japan calls its Northern Territories and says the Soviets seized illegally after Tokyo’s surrender at the end of World War II. Thousands of former Japanese residents of the islands are still alive, and resolving the dispute is a high priority for Japanese leaders. Russia’s activity on the islands, especially its military buildup, is therefore a sensitive issue for Tokyo.
Putin’s visit to the island Russia calls Iturup and Japan calls Etorofu on August 13 struck a chord with Tokyo not only for its location but also for its timing. Putin first traveled to Sakhalin Island – his first visit there in 13 years – to observe drills by Russia’s Pacific Fleet, part of a month-long series of exercises in the area that Japan protested. His visit also came days after the anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and days before the anniversary of Japan’s World War II surrender announcement.
Putin’s Kuril visit coincided with another Russian movement much farther south. The same day, Japan’s Defense Ministry reported that it had observed a Russian navy Improved Kilo-class submarine and a search-and-rescue vessel sailing north between the two Japanese islands closest to Taiwan, Yonaguni and Iriomote. That was one of at least 14 transits by Russian vessels around Yonaguni so far in 2026, a considerable increase over recent years.
A review of releases by the Japanese military’s Joint Staff from the past five years shows no such transits in 2021 and just two in 2022, both between Yonaguni and Iriomote. 2023 saw another two transits between Yonaguni and Iriomote, followed by a jump to six transits – five between Yonaguni and Iriomote and one between Yonaguni and Taiwan – in 2024. After a dip to four Yonaguni-Iriomote transits in 2025, there have been 11 transits between those islands and three between Yonaguni and Taiwan so far this year, the most recent on September 25.
Activity around Japan’s Southwest Islands is a growing concern for Tokyo. China has increased its military operations there since the early 2010s, training to sail and fly around and through that island chain. Chinese activity near Yonaguni and its neighboring islands, known as the Sakishima Islands, has also picked up in recent years, a sign of Beijing’s interest in familiarizing its forces with the area around Taiwan. In late 2024, a Chinese aircraft carrier sailed between Yonaguni and Iriomote for the first time, drawing a formal protest from Tokyo. In response, Japan has increased its military presence on the islands, opening bases for radars, electronic-warfare units, and surface-to-air and anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni and Ishigaki, which is just east of Iriomote.
Some Russian transits around Yonaguni appear to be part of routine voyages to and from the Pacific Fleet’s bases near Vladivostok. There may be a practical reason to use that route. “For ships coming south from Vladivostok through the East China Sea, the passage between Yonaguni and Iriomote provides a convenient way into the Philippine Sea without going farther northeast through the Miyako Strait,” Thomas Shugart, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security and a retired U.S. Navy officer, said in an email. Shugart said Russia’s navy may also have a political reason to avoid the more direct route to the South China Sea through the Taiwan Strait: “Given Beijing’s sensitivity to foreign naval transits of the Strait, routine Russian use could invite the observation that even the Russians treat it as an international waterway.”
But the behavior of other Russian vessels around Yonaguni appears more likely to be “deliberate signaling toward Japan,” Shugart said. In some cases, Russian vessels have loitered in the area, perhaps to monitor Japanese activity and response measures. In its annual “Defense of Japan” report, Japan’s Defense Ministry singled out an unusual operation in January this year, in which a Russian Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship was seen “navigating for an extended period” around the Sakishima Islands and Okinawa. Joint Staff releases showed that over the course of 12 days the vessel sailed south between Taiwan and Yonaguni and circled the Sakishima Islands before crossing the Miyako Strait and lingering southeast of Okinawa for three days. “Notably, this marked the first confirmed instance of such a vessel circumnavigating the Sakishima Islands,” the report said.
The ministry’s report linked recent activity around the Sakishima Islands with a years-long uptick in Russian operations around Japan, “including exercises and training likely intended to verify the results of military reforms” and operations farther afield that are likely meant to keep the U.S., Japan, and others “in check.”
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, its navy “has been continuously involved in active deterrent operations against the United States and its Western allies,” Alexey Muraviev, a professor at Edith Cowan University in Australia who studies Russian military strategy, said in an interview late last year. Regular deployments to Southeast Asia, where Moscow has sought to bolster its military ties, are a part of those operations, Muraviev said, but they also reflect continued concerns about the US and its allies, especially Japan. “Russia clearly sees Japan as a military risk – partially because of its alignment with the United States through security and defense ties, partially because of [the] unresolved territorial dispute,” Muraviev said.
Russia’s activity around Japan also shows its deepening military ties with China, which has become a more important partner amid Moscow’s international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine. Over the past several years, Sino-Russian bomber and naval patrols have incorporated a wider range of ships and aircraft, including diesel-electric submarines and nuclear-capable bombers, and traveled farther, sometimes circling the Japanese archipelago. During their most recent naval patrol, in July, their ships transited east through the Miyako Strait, headed north along Japan’s east coast, and then sailed west through the Vries Strait, which separates the Kuril Islands that Japan claims from the rest of the chain. The route demonstrated the two navies’ increasing ability to operate through “strategic waterways,” Chinese experts told state media.
Russia has also echoed China’s criticism of what it calls Japan’s “militarism,” a line of attack that Beijing started pushing late last year, likely in an attempt to stoke backlash to Japan’s growing military investments and regional security role. Russian officials returned to that talking point in the weeks following Putin’s visit to the Kuril Islands, lashing out at Japan for hosting a military exercise with the U.S. around Hokkaido, the Japanese main island closest to the Kurils, and objecting to its proximity to Russian territory. “The Japanese side was firmly informed that provocative military activity near our country’s far eastern borders is categorically unacceptable,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on September 1.

articles.title: ‘A Tower of Jelly’
articles.full_text:
The United Nations, U Thant, and the 1967 Arab-Israeli War.
U.N. Secretary-General U Thant (right) confers with Jose Rolz-Bennett, U.N. deputy chef de cabinet, and other officials during a session of the U.N. Security Council in New York, Sep. 3, 1963.
“What is the use of a fire brigade which vanishes from the scene as soon as the first smoke and flames appear?” asked Abba Eban, addressing an emergency session of the United Nations General Assembly soon after the 1967 Arab-Israeli War had ended.
In a fiery speech, the foreign minister of Israel lashed out at the U.N. for pulling peacekeeping troops out of the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip.  The “disastrously swift” withdrawal, Eban argued, had endangered the “national survival” of the Jewish state.
Israel’s Six-Day War was nevertheless a spectacular military success. The Israel Defense Forces neutralized three Arab armies (Egypt, Jordan, and Syria) within a week and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.
In his latest book, “Peacemaker,” historian Thant Myint-U offers new insights on the U.N.’s role in the events leading up to the six-day conflict.
The book’s title refers to U Thant, the author’s grandfather. As U.N. secretary-general, the Burmese diplomat was the chief “firefighter” charged with deploying peacekeeping troops to conflict zones.  The “most successful peacekeeping operation” was UNEF (United Nations Emergency Force), which had maintained a fragile peace along the border between Egypt and Israel for more than a decade.
When the Egyptian military sent the U.N. an informal communication in mid-May requesting a withdrawal of peacekeeping troops, Thant faced a dilemma. Denying Cairo’s request would violate Egypt’s sovereignty, but removing the forces might jeopardize the U.N.’s conflict-prevention mission.  The Secretary-General acquiesced after receiving an official letter from the foreign minister.  However, as Thant was negotiating UNEF’s exit, Israeli jets strafed a convoy in the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip, killing three soldiers.
Thant faced “a deluge of criticism” for the troop withdrawal and for his inability to counter “Egyptian bluster.”  Former British Prime Minister Alec Douglas-Home called the Secretary-General’s visit to Egypt in late May a “dreadful mistake.” When Thant landed in Cairo, President Gamal Abdel Nasser was already in war mode, having closed the Straits of Tiran, a vital shipping route for Israel.  A Western diplomat quoted in The Wall Street Journal called the U.N. chief “a tower of jelly.”
Gideon Rafael, the Israeli ambassador to the U.N., defended his friend in the Hebrew-language newspaper Maariv, saying, “U Thant is not responsible for the situation in the Middle East.”
In a chapter titled “Gaza and the Sinai,” the author highlights an intriguing detail on how misinformation played a role in the lead-up to the war.  Nasser’s actions were influenced by false intelligence reports relayed by Moscow and Damascus about a buildup of Israeli forces along the Syrian border.  Arab leaders did little to verify the claims, even as U.N. observers cast doubt on the report’s veracity.
“The Syrians could have looked from the Golan Heights (which they controlled) down into Israel and seen that there were no troop concentrations, as alleged, but they were happy to pass on to Cairo the misinformation as it confirmed their longstanding claim of an imminent threat,” commented the author.
In 1959, U Thant was the frontrunner for the top U.N. job as the only candidate acceptable to both Israel and the Arab states. Golda Meir, then Israel’s foreign minister, indicated that Thant was Tel Aviv’s sole choice for the position. However, the first Asian secretary-general of the U.N. did not have a “feel for the passions surrounding the conflict” once war broke out in the Middle East.
His low-key style worked when both parties were motivated to defuse a confrontation. During the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the U.N. Secretary-General helped create “an opening for diplomacy.”  U Thant “injected himself into the very heart of the simmering crisis,” the author wrote, giving the Soviet Union and the U.S. a face-saving option to back away from a nuclear showdown.  In 1965, the veteran diplomat was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for his mediation efforts.
The goodwill earned during his first term had evaporated by the late 1960s. In certain circles, Thant was considered “Israel’s nemesis,” and his relationship with Washington deteriorated. The secretary-general was a critic of the Vietnam War and spoke out against the Johnson Administration’s bombing campaign in Southeast Asia.
“Thant retired, then virtually disappeared,” wrote his grandson, almost as if he was “airbrushed from history.”
The former Secretary-General spent his final years in a colonial-style house outside New York City with “a meditation room, a glass-enclosed annex with images of the Buddha and views of the Westchester countryside.”

articles.title: Indonesian President Replaces Foreign Minister With Career Diplomat
articles.full_text:
The appointment of Arrmanatha Nasir is likely to result in a reassertion of the Foreign Ministry’s role in Indonesian foreign policymaking.
Arrmanatha Nasir, Indonesia’s vice minister for foreign affairs, speaks during the 16th session of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD16) in Geneva, Switzerland, Oct. 21, 2025.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has replaced his foreign minister with a career diplomat, in a cabinet reshuffle that saw more than a dozen other posts change hands.
In yesterday’s reshuffle, Prabowo appointed Arrmanatha Nasir, Indonesia’s former permanent representative to ‌the United Nations in New York, as the country’s new foreign minister. The outgoing foreign minister, Sugiono, was shifted to the post of coordinating minister for human development.
In this latest change to his “Red and White Cabinet,” Prabowo appointed three new coordinating ministers and a new minister of industry. He also reshuffled a handful of deputy ministerial posts and leadership positions at major government agencies, including the National Police and the office of the Ombudsman.
The changeover at the top of Kemlu, however, was the most significant position to change hands, and the second major cabinet change ​in the past few weeks.
In mid-September, Prabowo removed his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and replaced him with ​his deputy, Suahasil Nazara, amid growing investor concern about Indonesia’s economic trajectory.
Arrmanatha Nasir comes to the post with years of experience, having joined Kemlu in 1997. Since then, he has risen through the ranks, serving as the Ministry’s spokesperson between 2014 and 2019, Indonesia’s ambassador to France (2019-2021) and Indonesia’s ambassador to the U.N. (2021-2024). He was then appointed vice foreign minister when Prabowo took office.
After taking his oath of office yesterday, Arrmanatha said that his priorities included “maintaining ​stability in the region and promoting multilateralism,” Reuters reported.
Arrmanatha’s advent is likely to mark a significant change in the process of Indonesian foreign policymaking. His predecessor Sugiono was a political novice who came to the post with little hands-on experience in foreign affairs. While he served as the deputy head of the parliamentary commission overseeing foreign policy, his main credential was that he had served as deputy chairperson of Prabowo’s Gerindra Party.
Indeed, the appointment of such a junior figure appeared to mark a sharp break from the tenure of outgoing Foreign Minister Retno Marsudi, a career diplomat who had nearly two decades of experience in the diplomatic corps before her appointment as foreign minister in 2014.
The result has been that, in effect, if not in intention, the Foreign Ministry under Sugiono became largely subordinate to the presidential palace. As in the realm of economic policy-making, this has injected a degree of unpredictability into Jakarta’s foreign policy. As Trystanto Sanjaya, visiting fellow at the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs, posted on X, “Under Sugiono’s tenure, Indonesia’s Foreign Policy has been criticized as inconsistent and there has been reports where views of Indonesian diplomats are not considered when making important foreign policy decisions.”
Perhaps the most notable of these instances was the joint statement issued during Prabowo’s visit to Beijing in late 2024, which mentioned that the two countries had “reached important common understanding on joint development in areas of overlapping claims.”
The release of the joint statement was interpreted by some South China Sea watchers as marking a (perhaps unwitting) break from a long-standing Indonesian policy, and was quickly walked back by the Foreign Ministry. At the time, I argued that the incident “may represent less a conscious shift in policy than a cautionary tale about the perils of turning a nation’s foreign relations into a political sinecure.”
Dewi Fortuna Anwar, a foreign policy analyst at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency, told Reuters that Nasir, who was an “even-keeled” professional, would likely be more assertive in its relationship with the presidential palace. “He can be a foil to Prabowo,” she said.
Trystanto concurred that Nasir’s appointment “can be interpreted as a return to the traditional way of doing business at MoFA where the minister is appointed from within its ranks. However, will there be a return to the usual way of doing business regarding Indonesia’s Foreign Policy?” Given Prabowo’s bull-headed and unilateral style of governance, he wrote, “I am not too optimistic.”

articles.title: Can Kashmir Learn From India’s Gen Z Movement?
articles.full_text:
J&K has lost its statehood, local governance, and even the right to protest. But there is still a way to resist.
People gather during a protest organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, demanding accountability over alleged examination irregularities and education reforms, July 19, 2026.
On August 14, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah warned New Delhi of a potential Gen Z protest in the restive Himalayan region, while cataloguing the lieutenant governor’s endless attritions against his government – most recently the stalling on a reservation report that seeks to redress grievances over the open-merit category. On September 2, Abdullah’s Cabinet ministers descended onto Srinagar’s streets. Placards in hands, which named in bold, black letters the Narendra Modi regime’s repeated political incursions in Kashmir, they marched toward the headquarters of the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Hindu-nationalist party Modi heads. 
The demonstration was scuppered within minutes, with the police, which reports to the lieutenant governor, dashing on them. After a scuffle, the ministers were shoved inside vans like common criminals.
Scores of television crews and YouTubers captured the excess, but no outrage followed on India’s primetime television that evening. Protest in Modi’s India rarely finds coverage on TV, except when it spirals out of control, like it did during the farmers’ march to Delhi in 2020-2021, or this summer’s Gen Z outburst over medical entrance test paper leaks. But that is less coverage and more of salvage job for the government. Media coverage often seems designed to provoke anger against the protesters, who are almost always depicted as foreign funded and scheming to weaken the country’s territorial integrity. 
The dismantling of the idea of protest painfully and saliently stirs the question: how, then, does one keep a republic? This was a basic question asked by American Founding Father Benjamin Franklin. In 1789, when asked whether the Constitutional Convention had resulted in a republic or a monarchy, Franklin famously responded: “A republic, if you can keep it.” 
But Franklin had reason for optimism. He had lived through, even helped shape, a colony’s epoch-making transition into the first modern democracy, after expelling the then most powerful nation of the world. He was likely persuaded that of all the formidable guarantees that this new system bestowed to its people, the right to stir – and throw the government on a retreat – in the face of repression would be non-negotiable. 
Franklin was, of course, speaking without hindsight knowledge of multifarious assaults that eviscerated that right in several democracies. Steven Levitsky’s and Daniel Ziblatt’s 2018 book “How Democracies Die” provided a despairing elucidation how a band of demagogues succeeded in stymieing democratic push-backs, even as their regimes retained democracy’s outward trappings.
That paradox could not be more noticeable in contemporary Indian politics, especially in Kashmir, where Modi’s government has hubristically mounted campaigns to restrict federal rights. Since downgrading Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) to a union territory in the same decision that ended J&K’s partial autonomy in August 2019, the central government has dragged its feet on restoration of statehood. It has, at the same time, coercively erased dissent from Kashmir’s political lexicon.
A plurality of Indians approve of the government’s flagrant projection of force, and not merely because they have fallen for propaganda. Their rejection of dissent is, indeed, a measure of how deeply they are aligned with the BJP’s civilizational project which seeks not just to place Hindu interests on top in everyday political functioning, but to reclaim “Hindu pride” – which can mean anything from renaming roads, buildings, and cities, to erasing Mughal history from school textbooks, to creating conditions to dramatically erode Muslim representation in Parliament. 
In Kashmir, where Muslims cannot be precluded from being elected, power has been concentrated in the hands of a Hindu lieutenant governor (LG), Manoj Sinha, handpicked by New Delhi, through a series of government decrees that threaten India’s foundational underpinnings. Omar Abdullah opined in a recent podcast: “Earlier officers would find ten different ways of doing a task I ordered, now they find ten different reasons why it ought not be done.”
National Conference spokesperson Imran Dar hinted that there could be a design to make the local government unpopular. “The LG’s office is procrastinating unnecessarily on a serious issue related to students’ future… which can do considerable damage [to the government’s reputation],” he told The Diplomat. 
Sinha is an old brass of the BJP from Uttar Pradesh province, the theater of the Ram Janmabhoomi (birth place) movement. The culmination of the Ram Janmabhoomi agitations in a grand temple in January 2024 is Modi’s biggest selling point, besides Kashmir’s loss of autonomy.
Today, India’s secularist opposition coalition is palpably wary about entangling itself in Kashmir issues. That was not the case a few years ago, when opposition leader Rahul Gandhi signed off his Bharat Jodo Yatra in Srinagar, Kashmir’s capital, on an unexpectedly snowing, freezing January morning of 2023. Back then, Gandhi cited India’s syncretic traditions to re-etch the Muslim majority region more congenially in people’s minds. He talked of the parallels between shunyata, the concept of ego-less consciousness enshrined in Buddhism, and fanaa, the Sufi concept of annihilation of individual ego before God. 
Gandhi’s exhortation failed. In the April-May 2024 national elections, the BJP won both parliamentary seats in adjoining, overwhelmingly Hindu Jammu, and thereafter swept the region in the provincial election. The message that Gandhi, his Congress party, and its allies inferred was that prioritizing Muslim minorities’ grievances would be an invitation to derision and defeat at the ballot box.
That explains their current silence – not just on Kashmir but on many other hot-button issues of concern to Muslims, such as the incarceration of activist Umar Khalid, or even Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s “bulldozer thuggery” that largely targets Muslims. 
After Modi won his second term in 2019, he joked about the Congress’ inhibition. “In this election, not even a single political party could dare to mislead the country by wearing the mask of secularism,” he said. 
Waheed Para, a senior leader of the Jammu and Kashmir Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), says there is no reason to be “too dependent on the national parties” to advance J&K’s cause. He cited Ladakh’s successful push for negotiations with New Delhi, which was predicated on regional solidarities. However, Para pointed out that “the mandate is with the chief minister and we do not want to undermine that by taking initiative, though Mehbooba Mufti unsuccessfully wrote to him.” Mufti, a former chief minister herself, is the PDP president.
In December 2023, Modi’s government told the Supreme Court that it would restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood after elections were held in the region. It reneged on that promise, but no censure has ever come from the judiciary.
That abandonment by the central institutions makes an urgent case for political unity to be fostered within Kashmir. When you cannot rely on institutions, when you cannot rely on the national mood to soften, when the country’s secular allies are looking the other way, you have to rely on each other. This local unity, as Para pointed out, is what got traction for Ladakh’s own demands. 
To everyone’s bafflement, Kashmir is not doing that. Its political landscape is battered by daily one-upmanship – at public events, over carefully crafted podcasts, and more energetically on X, where some politicians choose to parade their superior moral fiber every day.
The common ground is the articulation of open scorn for the chief minister. Some of it is well deserved. Abdullah and his party promised 100,000 jobs to J&K’s unemployed youths besides restoration of Kashmir’s federal guarantees. On both counts its record is dismal, though that has to be judged in the context of his diminished authority. At any rate, reducing these fraught times into acerbic daily bulletins on a local government doesn’t help Kashmir. It helps individual ambitions. 
When Omar Abdullah assumed office two years ago, he knew his path would be arduous. What he faced was not just a pugnacious lieutenant governor’s hindrances to his office but the ideology that enabled such obstructionism. Hindu supremacy operates from 57,000 separate cells across India, and has more than 1.5 million volunteers spreading the ideology throughout India’s educational, political, and cultural spaces, intensifying tacit pressure on minorities, especially Kashmiris, to get used to their marginality. 
After taking office, Abdullah focused on repairing ties with New Delhi, hoping a calibrated navigation might be the key to negotiating federal concessions, or at least the flow of federal funds. Abdullah was right about the funds, but wrong about everything else. The BJP was prepared to cede nothing to him. It has gone too far promising an ideological pinnacle to its core constituency: the installation of a Hindu chief minister in Kashmir. The relegation of the Kashmiri Muslim leadership is necessary groundwork for that goal. 
Abdullah’s failure to be alarmed in time allowed a range of politicians to provoke public backlash against him, while casting themselves as J&K’s true champions. That posturing brought them instant adulation from Kashmir’s overwrought population, which wanted to pin its hope somewhere. These politicians have been sharing their resentment on everything from the Modi government’s controversial waqf legislation, to burgeoning liquor shops in Srinagar, to the Israel-U.S. war on Iran, but even more so about Abdullah’s National Conference’s linguistic timidity on these very flashpoints.
That is undoubtedly the right thing to do, but there is a problem. Kashmir’s self-appointed champions almost always deploy their dissidence from the protected perch of X, or to camera crews, not once outside the BJP’s headquarters or outside the Raj Bhavan, which would involve subjecting themselves to the police’s rough handling. For all the mixed reactions about their politics, Abdullah and Mufti are the only prominent politicians who have shown that grit – Abdullah when he forced his entry into the martyrs’ memorial in July 2025, and Mufti when she took the fight against encroachment to New Delhi’s streets in February 2023.
There are no dearth of people who are enamored with the new “dissidents.” But there are also those – small businessmen, entrepreneurs, academics, rural voters disengaged from the internet’s firestorm of opinions – who point out that emphasizing the need for dissidence is not itself dissidence. Upbraiding a disempowered local government for its lack of dissidence is not empowering. No one has yet articulated a sustainable political roadmap to actually achieve J&K’s goals, starting with restored statehood. 
That leaves Kashmir with motley emotions: fear, skepticism, despair, perhaps even a crestfallen urge in some to conform. Yet Sinha, the lieutenant government, depicts Kashmir as, in his own words, “at the threshold of a new future.” Roads, tunnels, and highways are being overhauled on a staggering budget. A digital economy and start-up culture are being imported from India’s metropolitan cities. Sinha sees a “cultural renaissance” unfolding, urging writers and thinkers to showcase “visionary craftsmanship.” 
Others see lived experiences obliterated with a crackdown on collective memory – Sinha banned 25 books last year. Sinha’s bureaucrats hear foot-tapping by an influx of tourists and movie crews; others hear collective gasping underneath that ebullient surface.
Despite this profound temptation to mourn, that cannot be the way forward. No political power is insurmountable in the long term. That universal principle should goad people to organize against it, while preserving hope, human will, solidarity for each other, and incorporation of those who are already fighting, in order to more coherently tap undercurrents of public disillusionment.
articles.summary: J&K has lost its statehood, local governance, and even the right to protest. But there is still a way to resist.

articles.title: As University of Tokyo Gets Its First Female President, How Far Is Japan From Gender Equality?
articles.full_text:
Fujigaki Yuko’s selection sparked controversy – and shone a light on Japan’s stubborn gender gap.
On September 28, 2026, Fujigaki Yuko was selected as the next president of the University of Tokyo. Following formal appointment by the minister of education, culture, sports, science, and technology, she will take office on April 1, 2027, for a six-year term.
As the university marks its 150th anniversary, Fujigaki will become the first woman to lead it. Yet at the institution she is about to head, only about one in five undergraduates is a woman.
Fujigaki is not Japan’s first female university president. In 1997, Niwa Masako became president of Nara Women’s University, the first woman to head a national university in Japan, and in 2001, Honda Masuko became the first female president of Ochanomizu University. Coeducational national universities also have earlier precedents: Ikehata Setsuho became the first female president of Tokyo University of Foreign Studies in 2001, and Kina Ikue became the first female president of the University of the Ryukyus in 2025. 
Even so, the appointment of a woman to lead the University of Tokyo, often seen as Japan’s most prominent university and an institution with considerable social influence, carries particular symbolic weight.
Fujigaki, 64, is a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, specializing in science and technology studies and scientometrics. She earned her bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees at the same university, completing her doctorate in 1990. Apart from nearly four years as a senior researcher at the government’s National Institute of Science and Technology Policy, she has spent her career at the university, becoming a professor in 2010. Starting in 2021, she served for five years as an executive vice president, overseeing areas including admissions, student support, and research ethics.
Her selection has nevertheless generated controversy both inside and outside the university. Most notably, Fujigaki did not receive the most votes in the university’s opinion vote. On September 28, eligible faculty and administrative staff took part in two rounds of voting, with the top three candidates in the first round advancing to the second. The vote was intended only as one source of information for the selection process and did not directly determine the final choice.
In the first round, Someya Takao, a professor at the Graduate School of Engineering, received 818 votes, or 38.0 percent of the 2,155 ballots cast, including blank ballots. Fujigaki received 400 votes, or 18.6 percent. In the second round, Someya received 1,107 votes, or 51.0 percent of the 2,169 ballots cast, while Fujigaki received 553, or 25.5 percent. Fujigaki therefore finished second in both rounds, with less than half as many votes as Someya. According to The Todai Shimbun, this appears to be the first time under the university’s established presidential selection system that a candidate who did not finish first in the opinion vote was ultimately chosen.
The final decision rested with the University President Screening & Inspection Committee. Half of its 16 members are chosen by the university’s Education and Research Council and include senior officials such as graduate school deans; the other half are external members of the university’s Administrative Council, with backgrounds in business, media, and other fields. Kuniya Hiroko, who chairs the committee, is a trustee of Tokyo University of the Arts and anchored NHK’s current affairs program “Close-up Gendai” for many years. The committee considers candidates’ policy statements, interviews, the opinion vote, and other materials before making its final decision.
Selecting the second-place candidate therefore did not violate the university’s procedures. But the committee’s authority to make the final decision does not eliminate the need to explain the gap between the vote and the eventual outcome. When one candidate receives majority support from participating faculty and staff but another is selected as president, members of the university can reasonably ask how much weight was given to the various criteria, what strengths outweighed the vote, and ultimately how much significance the university still attaches to its long-standing internal ballot.
In its statement, the committee said that through her experience as an executive vice president, Fujigaki had become keenly aware of the university’s role as a symbol of academia, and that she had the strong will and ability to restore trust in academia, drawing on her skill in communicating science and technology to the public. It also said that, drawing on her extensive international experience, Fujigaki had the ability to make the university more open by integrating the arts and sciences and strengthening communication within and beyond the university.
The committee’s reference to “restoring trust” has a clear context. In November 2025 and January 2026, an associate professor and a professor at the University of Tokyo Medical School Hospital were arrested on suspicion of bribery. The associate professor was accused of favoring a medical device company in procurement decisions and receiving roughly 700,000 yen (around $4,400) through a donation arrangement. The professor was accused of repeatedly accepting expensive entertainment, including at upscale clubs, from the head of an organization that had partnered with the university on a collaborative program. The university apologized, and the hospital director subsequently resigned.
At the same time, the University of Tokyo’s application to be designated a University for International Research Excellence, a status that would give it access to grants from the government’s University Fund, has remained under continued review since December 2025. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science, and Technology said the university still needed to clarify how it allocates resources and strengthen its institution-wide governance. Restoring trust and advancing governance reform are therefore important challenges for the next president.
Kuniya also said at the press conference that gender had not been a subject of discussion during the committee’s deliberations. 
It is important to distinguish questions about the transparency of the process from arguments about Fujigaki’s gender. Questioning how the selection was made does not amount to opposition to female leadership. Nor, in the absence of evidence, should the outcome simply be attributed to a preference for appointing a woman. Supporting more women in leadership and asking a university to explain a major personnel decision are not contradictory positions. 
At the same time, debates of this kind can reflect the unusually demanding standards sometimes applied to female leaders, making it important to remain alert to gender-based double standards.
Some critics have also compared Fujigaki’s academic record unfavorably with Someya’s. Japanese internet personality Nishimura Hiroyuki, for example, amplified claims on X that Someya’s papers had received roughly 70 times as many citations as Fujigaki’s. 
Someya is an engineer specializing in flexible electronics. His best-known work includes ultrathin electronic devices that can be attached directly to the skin. He has received numerous academic honors, including the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Prize in 2008, the Leo Esaki Prize in 2019, and the Fujiwara Prize in 2024, and has repeatedly appeared on Clarivate’s list of Highly Cited Researchers. Fujigaki, by contrast, mainly uses approaches from the humanities and social sciences to examine the relationship between science, technology, and society. 
Publication practices, research team size, language of publication, and citation patterns differ greatly across disciplines. Simply comparing total citation counts or numbers of awards therefore offers only a limited basis for judging the academic achievements of two scholars in different fields. 
More importantly, a university president is responsible not only for research but also for educational and research administration, organizational coordination, resource allocation, and public communication. Academic achievement is only one part of the selection criteria.
There is a broader context to the debate. Even as the University of Tokyo  prepares to install its first female president, the gender imbalance among its students remains pronounced. As of May 1, 2026, the university had 14,098 undergraduate students, of whom 3,023 were women – just 21.4 percent.
Across Japan, more than half of women now go on to university, but the overall figure conceals substantial inequalities between fields of study and stages of education. In 2025, 56.5 percent of women and 60.7 percent of men advanced to undergraduate programs, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. The gap becomes much wider at the graduate level: only 6.9 percent of female university graduates went directly on to graduate school, compared with 16.0 percent of men.
Differences by field are equally striking. In 2025, women accounted for 29.4 percent of undergraduates in science and just 17.9 percent in engineering. At the master’s level, their shares fell further, to 24.0 percent and 15.9 percent, respectively. The fact that more women are entering higher education does not mean that they participate equally across academic disciplines.
Women remain underrepresented at senior levels after entering academia as well. In 2025, women accounted for 28.2 percent of full-time faculty at Japanese universities and graduate schools, but only 20.1 percent of presidents, vice presidents, and professors. In 2024, just four of the 86 presidents of Japan’s national universities were women, or 4.7 percent, compared with 14.9 percent at public universities and 15.1 percent at private universities.
The same pattern is evident in corporate management. In 2025, women made up 16.1 percent of section managers and 9.3 percent of department managers at companies with at least 100 regular employees. As of October 2025, women headed only 8.6 percent of Japanese companies. Although this was a record high, the figure remained below one in ten.
Politics shows a similar imbalance. Takaichi Sanae became Japan’s first female prime minister in October 2025. Yet after Takaichi’s September 2026 Cabinet reshuffle, only three of the 19 Cabinet members, including the prime minister herself, were women. As of February 2026, women accounted for 30.0 percent of members of the House of Councillors but only 14.6 percent of members of the House of Representatives. These gaps show that women’s expanding access to higher education has not yet translated fully into representation in leadership and decision-making positions.
The appointment of the University of Tokyo’s first female president is symbolically important, but substantive progress will depend on what universities do to support women at different stages of their education and careers. That means encouraging women to continue into graduate education, supporting their participation in science and engineering, and creating classrooms in which they feel comfortable expressing their views and taking part in discussion. 
For researchers, it means reducing gender discrimination in the workplace, ensuring fair and transparent recruitment and promotion, and making it easier to combine research careers with caregiving responsibilities. Together, these measures can give women greater opportunities to develop their abilities and participate in decision-making, not only in academia but also in business and society more broadly.
On September 28, 2026, Fujigaki Yuko was selected as the next president of the University of Tokyo. Following formal appointment by the minister of education, culture, sports, science, and technology, she will take office on April 1, 2027, for a six-year term.
As the university marks its 150th anniversary, Fujigaki will become the first woman to lead it. Yet at the institution she is about to head, only about one in five undergraduates is a woman.
articles.summary: Fujigaki Yuko’s selection sparked controversy – and shone a light on Japan’s stubborn gender gap.

articles.title: Why Are Modi Government Critics Now Targeting India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
articles.full_text:
A recent investigative report strengthens opposition charges that the Modi government is using Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP.
Screenshot of a Congress party video showing its activists defacing the house of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Agra, India, Sept. 28, 2026.
“You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
“Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office.
Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago.
Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust.
The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders.
Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.
The opposition’s challenge to the law has not made much progress in the Supreme Court yet, with a five-judge constitutional bench expected to start hearing it.
The Indian Express report dropped like a political bombshell. Opposition parties jumped in to claim that the report vindicates what they have been alleging for a long time: that the BJP government is using Chief Election Commissioner Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP, starting with the voter roll.
Trying to downplay the internal rift, the commission’s reply was measured: differences are normal in any institution. Despite the concerns raised at different stages, the final decisions were unanimous, the commission said.
Its defense has not calmed the room. The Indian Express disclosures landed amid the highly contested overhaul of the voter roll, the Special Intensive Revision, which has removed millions of names from the electoral rolls. Several opposition leaders and civil society personalities, including Rahul Gandhi of the Congress, India’s main opposition party, have alleged that the electoral roll revision process is being used to steal votes.
A dispute inside a constitutional body has thus become evidence, for opponents, not only of a wider institutional failure, but also of “sabotage” of an institution that is most critical for the smooth functioning of an electoral democracy.
The CJP, a youth movement that spearheaded the July agitation, moved quickly. “Gyanesh, it’s done bro,” CJP leader Abhijit Dipke wrote on social media the day the Indian Express report was published. The CJP gave Kumar 48 hours to quit. In the national capital of New Delhi, the Jantar Mantar premises, the site of the June-July protests, were heavily barricaded on September 25 as organizations and activists, mostly leftists, marched. Several protesters were detained.
Opposition parties echoed the demand for Kumar’s resignation, accusing him of sidelining his fellow commissioners. Kumar, as expected, did not oblige.
Therefore, protests are expected in different parts of the country over the coming days, some led by the CJP, some by opposition parties. Over the past few days, Congress workers demonstrated in different states, with a rally outside the Election Commission’s office in the national capital.
The tension can perhaps be sensed from the fact that after some Congress workers defaced the gates and walls of Kumar’s residence in the BJP-ruled north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, police booked them under charges of attempt to murder.
While Kumar is the visible immediate target, the movement’s demands go further than one man’s exit. The CJP and opposition parties also want the entire SIR exercise to be scrapped. Gandhi asked people not to forget that it was Modi who appointed Kumar, which means the prime minister cannot escape responsibility for Kumar’s deeds and misdeeds.
BJP supporters argue that cleaning the rolls is a legitimate duty of the government. Some BJP leaders have even demanded that Kumar be awarded some of India’s highest civilian awards for his service in electoral reforms.
As a target, Kumar is much tougher to unseat than Pradhan. A minister serves at the government’s pleasure, and a prime minister can sacrifice one minister to defuse a larger crisis. A chief election commissioner’s position is designed to be harder to dislodge, because the office’s independence depends on that insulation. Article 324(5) gives the CEC the same removal protection as a Supreme Court judge.
That means a parliamentary motion on the grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity must be passed by special majorities in both houses of parliament. No such move has ever succeeded. Earlier this year, the chairpersons of both the upper and lower houses of Parliament rejected the opposition’s notice for Kumar’s removal.
Understandably, the Modi government would likely wait for the proceedings at the apex court, even as the ruling party is expected to garner public sympathy for Kumar and his “bold actions.”
The CJP and different student organizations and youth forces, on the other hand, seem to believe in the power of the street protests. To what extent the CJP, the student organizations, and opposition political parties manage to build sustained pressure through street protests remains to be seen. October being a month when festivals will be celebrated in most parts of the country, it would not be easy for them to maintain the momentum.
“You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
“Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office.
Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago.
Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust.
The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders.
Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.
The opposition’s challenge to the law has not made much progress in the Supreme Court yet, with a five-judge constitutional bench expected to start hearing it.
articles.summary: A recent investigative report strengthens opposition charges that the Modi government is using Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP.

articles.title: China’s Stake in the Russian Duma Elections
articles.full_text:
The topic is a controversial one in China due to the obvious parallels between the Russian and Chinese political systems and the stake the Chinese leadership has in the stability of their neighbor.
Russian President Vladmir Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping shake hands during Putin’s state visit to Beijing, May 20, 2026.
What did observers in China think about the Russian State Duma election on September 20? While retaining a veneer of democratic procedure, Vladimir Putin has steadily eliminated potential rivals and term limits, much like Xi Jinping has done. In past Russian election cycles, Chinese officials and experts by large have emphasized the importance of outcomes reinforcing political stability in Russia. 
In terms of the latest election, most Western commentary criticized the unfair process preventing Putin’s primary opposing party, Yabloko, from running. Yabloko – which means apple in Russian but actually is an acronym for the last names of its three founders –  is the only pro-democracy and anti-war party in Russia. By contrast, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun congratulated Russia for the “smooth conclusion” of the process and hailed the elections for representing “the will of the Russian people.” 
Chinese media commentary did note that Yabloko was prohibited from participating in the election as a party, although some Yabloko candidates were still running in single-member districts (and all lost). Given the lack of real electoral competition, a Hong Kong media outlet, China Review News Agency, pointed out that the 59 percent turnout (7.6 percentage points higher than the previous Duma election in 2021) reflected “the state’s mobilization capabilities,” not increased political participation. 
Putin’s televised address in the lead-up to the election framed it as an opportunity for Russians to express their support for the war in Ukraine and as “a collective response to those who seek to weaken Russia,” Chinese commentary reported. More than 200 Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine ran for the Duma and election commission chair Ella Pamfilova reported that 46 of them won seats – 41 of whom belonged to United Russia, the ruling party that has dominated the Russian political landscape throughout Putin’s leadership. 
With the elections held against a background of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian soil and rising prices, Ma Bin, deputy director of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Fudan University, called the Duma election a major test and demonstration of Russian political stability. Chinese military analyst Shi Hong agreed that United Russia’s overwhelming victory demonstrated that for Russia “stability was paramount” and would support continuity in Russia’s military strategy and appropriations. Zhang Yanjun, a research fellow at the Institute of International Studies in Shanghai, predicted that the results of the election (held for the first time on occupied Ukrainian territory) would make Putin more intent on demonstrating strategic resolve and less likely to make concessions on Ukraine.
Since the failed coup attempt by the (since deceased) Wagner Group chairman, Yevgeny Prigozhin, in 2023, Chinese officials have made some efforts to reach out to officials beyond Putin’s inner circle. Wu Dahui, deputy director of the Russian Research Institute at Tsinghua University, emphasized that the Sino-Russian partnership has become institutionalized in a dense network of 60,000 channels at all levels of society, which he likened to the “blood vessels” sustaining the partnership. 
Nevertheless, recently Chinese and Russian officials have emphasized the importance of top leader ties for their partnership. Following their most recent summit in May 2026, a Chinese diplomat hailed the relationship between Xi and Putin as “the fundamental guarantee” of the partnership. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov credited the “diplomacy of leaders” for codifying progress in the partnership in concrete agreements. 
With the Russian ruling party, United Russia, capturing the majority of seats in the latest election (349 out of 450), Guo added that China would continue to work with Russia to implement “the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.”
A 2019 article by Professor Wang Zhihua in the Rule of Law Forum of the Shanghai University of Political Science and Law about the role of the Duma in the Russian political system noted that in the Russian system the president has “absolute power” and constitutionally outlined checks and balances are “merely nominal, resulting in a unique presidential system with Russian characteristics.” Wang concluded that “In short, in Russia’s political system, the president has too much power, the parliament has less power, and the judiciary is also weak.” 
In Wang’s view, the configuration of the Russian political system based on a strong president with personal charisma may be expedient in the short term for the country’s revival and rise. However, he cautioned that the expansion of presidential power may ultimately lead to a crisis and undermine the long-term development of legally based governance. 
Such conclusions could easily be applied to China and it is not surprising that this article, which I obtained on September 11, 2026, is no longer accessible on the CNKI database of academic articles and or on the Baidu search engine. 
Chinese scholars’ assessments of Russian political developments also contribute to our understanding of Chinese views about the long-term viability of the Sino-Russian partnership. An analysis of the Duma election by a Chinese military blogger emphasized the importance of Putin’s continued hold on power and his ability to restrain hardline factions from even more escalatory actions in Ukraine. The blogger wrote: “For China, while the specific choice of Russian leader is important, Russia’s ability to maintain stability and policy continuity is even more crucial. This is why Sino-Russian relations have been continuously strengthening institutional ties in recent years.”
The results of the Russian Duma election startled no one in Beijing, but Chinese observers followed them closely. articles.title: Taiwan Can’t Fight Beijing’s History War While Erasing Its Own ROC Legacy
articles.full_text:
The push to emphasize Taiwanese identity is at odds with the government’s attempt to center the Republic of China in World War II history.
At last week’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the White House described the United States and China as World War II allies who “fought side by side to win the war.” It was a small phrase with a large omission. The government that represented China during the war, and fought alongside the United States against Japan, was the Republic of China (ROC). The government Xi leads – the People’s Republic of China (PRC) – did not exist until 1949, four years after Japan’s surrender. By collapsing the two into a single, unbroken “China,” the summit’s language risked allowing the PRC to inherit the legacy of a war it did not fight.
Taiwan’s government noticed. Its Mainland Affairs Council pushed back, insisting that the ROC was the “true ally” that fought with the United States during the war, and emphasizing that the PRC did not even exist during World War II. Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung went further, calling the framing an act of “de-ROC-ization” – in which the Republic of China’s very existence is being erased from history, and replaced by the Chinese Communist Party. “We should feel very distressed,” Wu added. 
Taiwanese scholars echoed the concern, warning that if Washington adopts Beijing’s version of events, the result could be a further hollowing out of the ROC’s place in the historical record.
There is an obvious irony in Taipei’s complaint, however. Taiwan’s government has been taking steps to distance itself from the ROC moniker.
This year, Taiwan’s representative office in Los Angeles sent out National Day invitations branded “Taiwan National Day.” The previous year’s cards had read “Republic of China 114th National Day.” The same government whose deputy foreign minister accused Beijing of erasing the ROC internationally was removing references to the ROC from its own diplomatic correspondence.
This trend also impacts how Taiwan’s government speaks about World War II. In August 2025, marking the 80th anniversary of Japan’s surrender, President Lai Ching-te referred to the occasion as the “end of the war” (終戰), rather than using the more traditional ROC-centered formulation, “victory in the War of Resistance” (抗戰勝利). Lai’s message emphasized the broader lessons of aggression, unity, and victory. Opposition lawmakers criticized the omission of the ROC’s wartime role, interpreting the terminology as part of a broader shift toward a more Taiwan-centered historical narrative.
The term “end of the war” is not new to Taiwan’s official vocabulary, nor does its use prove an effort to erase the ROC. But the choice of terminology in a major 80th anniversary commemoration illustrates a broader evolution in how Taipei frames the war and Taiwan’s place in it. The “Republic of China (Taiwan)” formulation associated with the Tsai Ing-wen era, together with Lai’s subsequent emphasis that the ROC and the People’s Republic are “not subordinate to each other,” has produced a more Taiwan-centered conception of ROC sovereignty. Critics argue that this can weaken the salience of the ROC’s pre-1949 history, the period when it controlled mainland China, even as Taipei continues to invoke the ROC as a sovereign state distinct from the PRC.
Successive Taiwanese governments have had domestic and diplomatic reasons to soften the ROC’s historical claims: a citizenry that increasingly identifies as Taiwanese rather than Chinese, a desire to avoid unnecessarily entangling Taiwan’s future with the mainland’s history, and a preference for language that does not appear to revive a rival claim to “all of China.” 
The argument here is not that Taiwan’s evolving democratic identity is morally equivalent to Beijing’s historical revisionism. One is the normal evolution of a pluralist society’s self-understanding; the other is a state-backed effort to shape historical memory in ways that support a broader political narrative. But the two are not unrelated, either. 
Taiwan’s own retreat from ROC symbolism complicates its ability to contest Beijing’s framing of “China.” It can narrow the space in which Taiwan is willing to defend the ROC’s history and identity, leaving more room for Beijing to present its own account of China’s wartime and postwar history.
Taipei has repeatedly emphasized that the PRC has never ruled Taiwan, and it has invoked the ROC’s historical continuity, as well as postwar arrangements including the San Francisco Peace Treaty, in making its case against Beijing’s territorial claims. These arguments depend in part on Taiwan being understood internationally as a political entity with its own historical trajectory – including a wartime and postwar history distinct from that of the PRC.
That creates a strategic paradox. The more Taipei reduces the visibility of the ROC’s historical identity in its own diplomatic and commemorative practice, the less salient that historical continuity may become internationally. This does not automatically strengthen Beijing’s legal case or alter Taiwan’s sovereignty. But it can give Beijing greater narrative space to portray the wartime “China” as an uninterrupted predecessor of today’s PRC, while making the ROC’s alternative historical continuity harder to communicate.
I have argued elsewhere that Taiwan’s assertion of sovereignty in its own waters suffers from a similar underlying problem: not insufficient assertiveness, but the absence of a coherent doctrine explaining when and why Taipei invokes its own claims. The same logic applies here. Beijing is contesting the historical identity of “China” itself, using the Trump-Xi summit as one more venue in which to do so.
Taiwan is right to object to historical formulations that erase the ROC’s role in World War II. But an objection becomes harder to sustain when the government’s own recent practice – from diplomatic invitations to commemorative language to evolving formulations of national identity – makes the ROC’s historical identity less visible.
None of this means Taiwan must reverse its democratic evolution or resurrect a mainland-centric ROC identity that most Taiwanese people no longer want. It does mean that Taipei cannot simultaneously retire the ROC as an inconvenient historical label and rely on it as part of the foundation of its case against Beijing. If Taiwan wants the ROC’s history to remain a live argument against the Chinese Communist Party’s claims to sovereignty over Taiwan, someone has to keep making that argument – including, consistently, the government in Taipei itself.

articles.title: Australia as an AI Middle Power
articles.full_text:
As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of change.
Australia’s role in the frontier world of artificial intelligence was the focus in Canberra last month, with two events bringing together hundreds of defense, diplomacy, development, and industry experts. The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) gathered the national security and defense community for an AI Masterclass on September 14. The next day, the Development Intelligence Lab’s Situation 2026 explored how AI can solve Indo-Pacific development challenges.
The events revealed a country grappling with what it means to be a middle power in the age of AI. As ClearAI founder Jisoo Kim put it, at a time when AI is developing at breakneck speed and reordering economies and societies, “Where in this ecosystem, where in this global economy is Australia going to sit?”
Judging from opinion polling, many Australians would probably prefer that AI had never been invented. But now that the cat is out of the bag, Australia needs to think about what it means for its security and prosperity, and the risks and opportunities it brings.
As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of these changes. It has some capacity to influence the new world that AI is making.
Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton addressed this openly. Asking how middle powers manage AI, he identified four plays: alignment with a superpower, leverage in the value chain, competition through different models and capabilities, and sovereign capability. Charlton stated that Australia is pursuing all four simultaneously.
Shadow Minister for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie broadly agreed, particularly emphasizing the U.S. relationship as Australia’s “line to sovereignty.” Hastie suggested using Australia’s relationships in Washington to encourage a hyperscaler to invest in Australia. 
Without data centers, frontier labs, and talent, Australia remains dependent on what comes through submarine cables, and this may make Australia a “supplicant state” – with Hastie using the analogy of the nuclear race, where once the U.S. convinced Australia to withdraw, it has been reliant on Washington ever since. He gave a sense of the stakes for Australia: countries with AI will pull ahead and Australia will fall further behind. 
According to Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres, the government’s “aim is not to do everything, but to make ourselves the indispensable country.” That is, to find what Australia can excel at in this new ecosystem and make it the country’s comparative advantage. 
Australia brings assets in policy expertise, talent, and trust. Ayres also highlighted capabilities in chip packaging, quantum computing, and specialized datasets, alongside institutional advantages such as firms and unions working together in the national interest.
Throughout the discussions, there were multiple calls for Australia to work with other countries including the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and India.
As the American Enterprise Institute’s Ryan Fedasiuk put it, middle powers have a path forward if they “conceive of AI as a global megaproject which everyone can contribute to.” Importantly, “Sovereignty doesn’t mean autarky. Sovereignty means being able to choose your own dependencies rather than having them foisted on you.”
Aditya Maheshwari of the Indian Institute of Management Indore outlined how middle powers could energize their own ecosystems through talent, research, joint projects, and shared computing facilities, rather than competing with the United States and China on frontier models.
Australia also has considerable opportunities to shape international standards. Australian Signals Directorate Director-General Abigail Bradshaw argued that having a place in the AI industry strengthens Australia’s sovereignty and gives it a voice in global standards.
Australian AI Safety Institute head Kate Conroy highlighted Australia’s ability to punch above its weight internationally, drawing on its experience in developing standards adopted globally. 
Australia’s Ambassador for Cyber Affairs and Critical Technology, Jessica Hunter, argued that Australia has the assets, relationships, and agency to be a shaper of the AI world rather than merely a consumer.
It’s interesting that this proactivity is being actively encouraged by frontier labs, including OpenAI Vice President Ann O’Leary and Anthropic Special Envoy and former U.S Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich.
An important element of being an AI middle power is to think about how it contributes to development outcomes. As Minister for International Development Anne Aly put it, “The value of technologies lies in the way that people’s lives are improved.” The challenge is “to ensure the benefits of emerging technologies are shared widely rather than used to widen inequalities.” 
Through this lens, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sponsored a competition on what Indo-Pacific development challenge AI could solve in the next five years, gathering more than 100 proposals. From disaster warning systems to healthcare and protecting Pacific maritime zones, there are countless ways Australia can use AI to contribute as a development partner. 
Times of change are generally good for middle powers, enabling them to play an entrepreneurial role. These discussions demonstrated the benefits of Australia inserting itself into the AI economy, shaping global safety standards and enabling positive diffusion of technology across the region.

Without data centers, frontier labs, and talent, Australia remains dependent on what comes through submarine cables, and this may make Australia a “supplicant state” – with Hastie using the analogy of the nuclear race, where once the U.S. convinced Australia to withdraw, it has been reliant on Washington ever since. He gave a sense of the stakes for Australia: countries with AI will pull ahead and Australia will fall further behind. 
According to Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres, the government’s “aim is not to do everything, but to make ourselves the indispensable country.” That is, to find what Australia can excel at in this new ecosystem and make it the country’s comparative advantage. 
Australia brings assets in policy expertise, talent, and trust. Ayres also highlighted capabilities in chip packaging, quantum computing, and specialized datasets, alongside institutional advantages such as firms and unions working together in the national interest.
Throughout the discussions, there were multiple calls for Australia to work with other countries including the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and India.
articles.summary: As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of change.

articles.title: The New Development Bank Quietly Delivers During India’s BRICS Year
articles.full_text:
India is in a unique position as a founding member and one of its biggest borrowers.
The headquarters of the New Development Bank in Shanghai, China.
As India hosted the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, a familiar question returned: does the grouping produce anything beyond summit statements? The New Development Bank (NDB) offers the clearest evidence in the affirmative. India first proposed the bank at an earlier BRICS summit in New Delhi in 2012, and its 2026 chairship of BRICS brought that idea full circle. 
Judging a development bank is not simple; big announcements matter less than the money that actually reaches projects. The NDB’s record can thus be evaluated on three broad counts. The first is how much it has lent and how much of that money has actually been paid out. The second is whom the bank lends to. The third is how it raises the money it lends. On all three, the picture is more encouraging than the NDB’s low public profile suggests. 
By the end of June 2026, the NDB had approved loans worth about $44 billion for 141 projects in clean energy, transport, water systems and digital infrastructure. Of that amount, roughly $25 billion had already been paid out to borrowers. The second figure is especially important. Many development banks approve large loans but pay out much less, and much more slowly. A bank that has paid out more than half of what it approved is doing real work, not just signing agreements. 
The NDB’s public figures show what this money is building: 2,400 megawatts of clean energy capacity under way, 1,400 kilometers of tunnels and canals, 43 schools built or upgraded and a large increase in sewage treatment capacity. 
The bank’s reach has also grown. Its founding members were Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It has since added Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. Its members now stretch from South and Central Asia to Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America. 
India’s place in the NDB is unusual. It helped create the bank, it owns an equal share of it, and it is one of its biggest borrowers. Each founding member holds about 18.7 percent of the bank’s capital. This was designed so that no single country could control it. Even so, India has used the bank’s loans more than most members. 
Since 2016 the bank has approved 32 initiatives for India, worth close to $9.5 billion, in transport, social development, and clean energy. Lending has continued into 2026 also. Recent approvals include a $300 million clean energy project involving REC Limited and an affordable housing project backed by the Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO). Earlier, the bank provided $500 million towards the 82-km long rapid transit line between Delhi and Meerut. This is not aid. It is an ordinary lending relationship. 
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has described the NDB’s value less in terms of money and more in terms of shared knowledge. In August 2026, she said development banks should help countries plan cities and infrastructure better, not just pay for them. NDB President Dilma Rousseff, a former president of Brazil, replied by pointing to India’s Viksit Bharat development plans as a model for other members. It is a small but telling detail: the bank India proposed is now led by a Brazilian who uses Indian policy as an example for everyone else. 
The third count, how the bank funds itself, is where India’s chairship of BRICS this year has left its clearest mark. In August 2026, the bank and the Indian government held a joint meeting on bringing more private money into development projects. Rousseff called this a key priority, as members look for ways to fund large infrastructure beyond what governments alone can pay for. Sitharaman’s point was simple: development banks can make projects safer and more predictable for private investors, which brings in more private money. 
Two more steps followed. On September 10, two days before the BRICS summit opened, the bank raised 7 billion Chinese yuan through a bond sale in China. This gave it a new source of funds, separate from its usual channels. On the same day, it launched a BRICS-NDB knowledge portal linked to India’s chairship. 
These steps will not make headlines outside financial circles. But they matter. A bank that can raise money in different markets and attract private investors does not have to wait for its member governments to put in more capital. That makes it a more reliable lender for developing countries. At the same time, however, relying more on Chinese bond markets may raise questions about whether the bank’s funding is spread evenly across its members. 
The NDB can be an important source of finance for the Global South, helping countries build power plants, transport links and water systems. But development lending is slow work. It needs steady funding, careful planning, and trust between members. India’s chairship year has pushed the bank toward a broader funding base. Whether that shift lasts will become clearer in 2027, when India will host the bank’s annual meeting and this year’s results can be measured against what follows.
