articles.title: Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
articles.full_text:
Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan.
Japanese vessels conduct mine warfare training in Mutsu Bay, Jul 16, 2023.
On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved.
Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
The first lesson of the Iran war is that the traditional approach of waiting until a crisis escalates before evacuating people is no longer sufficient. Even before the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese government had warned of the deteriorating situation in Iran and encouraged Japanese nationals to leave early. Once the fighting began, however, it became necessary to confirm the safety of Japanese nationals and assist with their departure not only in Iran but also across neighboring areas, including Israel, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates. 
In March, the Japanese government supported multiple overland evacuations from Tehran to Azerbaijan and also assisted Japanese nationals in Gulf countries with their return home. Importantly, these evacuations were not carried out solely by Self-Defense Forces aircraft or charter flights; they relied on a combination of overland routes, commercial aviation, and transit through third countries.
An even larger problem was the temporary degradation of airports and airspace across the Gulf, including major hubs such as Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Doha. Dubai is not simply one airport in the Middle East; it is one of the world’s leading aviation hubs linking Asia with Europe and Africa. Disruption there complicated movement not only for people evacuating Iran and Israel but also for travelers and foreign residents throughout the Gulf. The experience demonstrated once again that a crisis may not remain confined within the borders of one country and can quickly engulf regional transportation hubs.
This lesson applies directly to a Taiwan contingency. In peacetime, large numbers of Japanese nationals are in Taiwan for tourism, business, study, and long-term assignments. Once hostilities begin, not only Taiwan’s airports and ports but also the surrounding airspace and waters could become dangerous. Transportation in Hong Kong, coastal China, Okinawa, and the Sakishima Islands could also be affected. In other words, a plan designed only to move Japanese nationals out of Taiwan would be insufficient. Japan must prepare for a scenario in which multiple transportation nodes across East Asia become unavailable at the same time.
Within Japan, civil protection plans to evacuate residents and tourists from the Sakishima Islands to Kyushu and Yamaguchi have become increasingly concrete, with field exercises scheduled for fiscal year 2026. This is an important development. Yet civil protection planning primarily concerns the evacuation of people inside Japan. By contrast, the evacuation of Japanese nationals from Taiwan, Hong Kong, coastal China, and other overseas locations spans several frameworks, including consular assistance by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, transportation under the Self-Defense Forces Act, and the securing of civilian transportation. If domestic evacuation and overseas evacuation occur simultaneously, Japan would still face the unresolved question of how to allocate aircraft, ships, airports, and ports between the two missions.
The lesson from the Iran War is not simply that Japan should increase the transport capacity of the Self-Defense Forces. Moving tens of thousands of people within a short period ultimately depends on cooperation with commercial airlines, shipping companies, airports and ports, and third countries. Japan therefore needs, in peacetime, to identify which civilian services could be maintained during a crisis, which third countries could serve as evacuation hubs, and which ports could be used if air routes were closed. 
Plans must also address how to provide shelter, food, communications, and medical care for those who cannot be evacuated immediately. An evacuation plan cannot consist only of a plan for getting people out; it must also include a plan for keeping them safe until evacuation becomes possible.
Ensuring Safe Navigation Without Becoming a Party to the Conflict
The second challenge is how to ensure the safety of maritime traffic. During the Iran War, the Strait of Hormuz was not completely closed, but normal commercial navigation became extremely difficult because of the risk of attacks on and seizures of merchant vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, Iranian traffic control measures, and the U.S. blockade of Iran. 
In June, the United States and Iran reached a memorandum of understanding that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Japanese government also called for the early restoration of free and safe navigation. Yet even in late September, traffic through the strait remained well below prewar levels. 
On September 22, Iran indicated that it was prepared to reopen the strait quickly if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. This, in turn, shows that as of late September, the restoration of safe navigation remained a matter of diplomatic and military negotiation. 
This raised a further question: who should be responsible for ensuring safe navigation? If the United States, as a party to the conflict, leads convoy escorts or other maritime operations, participating states are more likely to be perceived as having been militarily incorporated into the U.S. side. Yet civilian shipping cannot simply be left exposed in dangerous waters. 
European states have therefore sought arrangements that would protect freedom of navigation while maintaining a degree of distance from U.S.-led operations. In September, France was reported to be considering a United Nations Security Council resolution for an international mission to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Such an approach can be understood as an attempt to distinguish, as far as possible, alliance military operations from the protection of maritime traffic as an international public good.
A similar dilemma would arise in a Taiwan contingency. If the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters became dangerous, maintaining maritime traffic would be a major economic and security concern for Japan. Yet the threshold for participation would be extremely high if measures to protect shipping could immediately lead to armed conflict with China. What is needed is an institutional distinction, to the greatest extent possible, between joining combat operations and supporting the safe navigation of civilian vessels. Japan should therefore clarify in advance options that are not integrated into the use of force, including post-ceasefire mine clearance, information sharing, sea-lane monitoring, rescue of vessels in distress, and cooperation with escort frameworks led by third countries.
This issue is also related to the limits of Japan’s 2015 Legislation for Peace and Security. The legislation permits the minimum necessary use of force only when the so-called three new conditions are satisfied, including cases in which an armed attack on a foreign country that is in a close relationship with Japan poses a clear threat to Japan’s survival and to the fundamental rights of its people. It is important to note that, as a matter of law, U.S. participation in a conflict is not itself a requirement for recognizing a situation that threatens Japan’s survival. The Japanese government has also stated with regard to a Taiwan contingency that whether a particular situation constitutes such a threat must be determined comprehensively in light of the specific circumstances actually arising. It is therefore inaccurate to frame the issue as one in which Japan can do nothing unless the United States participates.
However, what is legally possible and what can actually be recognized in practice are different questions. A situation threatening Japan’s survival can be recognized only when there is a clear danger to Japan’s existence and to the rights of its people, and when no other appropriate means are available. Disruption to maritime traffic or higher resource prices alone would not automatically meet that threshold. 
Moreover, when Japan seeks to secure safe navigation in a manner that is not directly connected to combat with the opposing state, the framework of a situation threatening Japan’s survival may in some cases be too weighty. In March 2026, views were expressed within the Japanese government that minesweeping in the Strait of Hormuz after a ceasefire could be considered as one option. This is one example of the importance of maritime security measures that are institutionally separated from direct participation in combat.
The same perspective should guide discussion of a Taiwan contingency. The debate should not be reduced to a binary question of whether Japan would exercise the right of collective self-defense. Japan instead needs to strengthen the legal and institutional arrangements that apply before that threshold is reached and in adjacent areas. Specifically, it should clarify the legal basis and timing for measures such as the evacuation of Japanese nationals, maritime security, mine clearance, information sharing, warnings to civilian vessels, coordination with third countries and international organizations, and the alternative use of ports and airports. A U.N. resolution or an international framework led by third countries could be one option. Yet because China is a permanent member of the Security Council and possesses a veto, it would be unrealistic to rely solely on a U.N. resolution. Japan therefore needs multiple legal and diplomatic pathways.
What Should Japan Learn From the Iran War?
The Iran-U.S. war became a major crisis that simultaneously challenged the protection of Japanese nationals and the security of maritime transportation. It demonstrated that preparing for contingencies cannot be reduced to the question of how far the Self-Defense Forces can be used. In the initial phase of a crisis, airport closures and airspace restrictions may halt civilian transportation, while the population requiring evacuation may rapidly expand from the belligerent state to neighboring countries. At sea, Japan may be called upon to help ensure safe navigation even without participating in hostilities, while still facing the risk that such activity could be interpreted as support for one of the parties to the conflict.
The same problems could arise in a Taiwan contingency. The central issue is not to reduce a Taiwan crisis immediately to the questions of a situation threatening Japan’s survival or the exercise of collective self-defense. Rather, Japan needs to institutionalize and operationalize the measures that would become necessary before such a determination: the evacuation of Japanese nationals, the evacuation of residents, the maintenance of air and maritime transportation, protection of sea lanes, and cooperation with third countries. The Iran war has revealed a new “intermediate domain” within the legal and institutional framework Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
Diplomatic efforts to prevent a Taiwan contingency must of course continue. Yet considering what should be done if deterrence fails is also part of security policy. The most important lesson Japan should draw from the Iran War is that the issue should not be framed as a binary choice between participation and non-participation in war. Instead, the many practical tasks that lie between those two poles must be institutionalized in advance.
On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. articles.title: Central Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Act on Display from Bishkek to New York
articles.full_text:
Central Asia aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations.
The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds.
Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.”
Taken together, the two gatherings reveal a clear division of labor in Central Asian diplomacy. The region’s governments echo Beijing’s and Moscow’s grievances in regional group settings like the SCO, court Washington with concrete deals via bilateral channels, and use the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) podium to say as little as possible that might offend any of the three.
The balancing starts with who showed up. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Emomali Rahmon, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, and Sadyr Japarov all attended the SCO summit in person, alongside China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi. Three weeks later, only Japarov traveled to New York, after making a stop in the U.S. state of Utah. All five Central Asian countries had sent their heads of state last year for the U.N.’s 80th anniversary. Xi and Modi also skipped this year’s session, though Xi was in Washington on a state visit around the same time.
This does not mean, however, that Central Asia has abandoned Washington for its rivals. Kazakhstan, for one, backed Security Council Resolution 2803, the November 2025 measure endorsing Trump’s Gaza peace plan and his Board of Peace, even though Russia and China abstained. Tokayev sits on that board. Kazakhstan, which announced it would join the Abraham Accords last November, also took part in its first accords meeting in New York on September 24. Japarov, for his part, carried the SCO’s complaint about Western sanctions to the UNGA podium, yet he also thanked Trump for cutting U.S. funding to foreign NGOs.
These are low-cost gestures aimed at a transactional White House, and they come bundled with commerce. In mid-October, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will lead a delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand for a C5+1 ministerial meeting, his first trip to the region. With the United States and China racing to secure critical minerals, Central Asian capitals have something Washington wants.
Beijing, meanwhile, offers trade on a scale Washington cannot match. Xi paired the Bishkek summit with a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and pledged an SCO center for AI cooperation and 100 joint technology projects over three years. He arrived as the region’s largest trading partner, after China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record $106 billion last year. In Bishkek, all four Central Asian members also reaffirmed their support for China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Competition between the two powers lets Central Asian capitals bargain with both.
Central Asia is also building influence inside the U.N. system, and the great power scramble for its mineral wealth may give it more leverage to raise its global profile. Kyrgyzstan joins the Security Council in January, having been elected with 142 votes in June. Tajikistan used its UNGA address to announce its first-ever U.N. Security Council bid, for 2028-2029. Uzbekistan declared its candidacy for 2035-2036 and will chair the Non-Aligned Movement next year, while Turkmenistan will chair the group of landlocked developing countries.
Uzbekistan’s statement, delivered by the president’s daughter and head of the presidential administration Saida Mirziyoyeva, captured the balancing act neatly. Observing that countries are being asked which side they choose, Mirziyoyeva answered with “human dignity” rather than a camp, echoing the Bishkek Declaration’s own rejection of “bloc-based and confrontational” approaches. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev sat beside Xi and Putin in Bishkek; next month, Samarkand hosts Rubio.
Central Asia’s multivector strategy has not disappeared, but it has changed form. The region now aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations. As great power rivalry intensifies, the open questions are how long Central Asian governments can hold this position and how much they can gain from it.

Uzbekistan declared its candidacy for 2035-2036 and will chair the Non-Aligned Movement next year, while Turkmenistan will chair the group of landlocked developing countries.
Uzbekistan’s statement, delivered by the president’s daughter and head of the presidential administration Saida Mirziyoyeva, captured the balancing act neatly. Observing that countries are being asked which side they choose, Mirziyoyeva answered with “human dignity” rather than a camp, echoing the Bishkek Declaration’s own rejection of “bloc-based and confrontational” approaches. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev sat beside Xi and Putin in Bishkek; next month, Samarkand hosts Rubio.
Central Asia’s multivector strategy has not disappeared, but it has changed form. The region now aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations. As great power rivalry intensifies, the open questions are how long Central Asian governments can hold this position and how much they can gain from it.
The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds.
Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.”
Bimal Adhikari, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of political science and international relations at Nazarbayev University.
Zhuldyz Gabdsattarova is an undergraduate student at Nazarbayev University majoring in political science and international relations.
Arailym Munaitpas is an undergraduate student at Nazarbayev University majoring in computer science with a minor in political science and international relations.
articles.summary: Central Asia aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations.

articles.title: Officials Detained as Kazakhstan Mourns Soldiers Perished at Sea
articles.full_text:
Five military officials were arrested in connection to the deaths of 14 servicemen lost at sea during a combat exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan, as a day of national mourning is observed.
Kazakhstan is mourning the deaths of 14 servicemen who were lost during a military drill. The tragedy took place on September 24 during the 2026 Caspian Defense exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan. The episode has led to the dismissal of the defense minister, while five officials are being investigated for negligence in relation to the case.
According to the Kazakh Ministry of Defense, a total of 17 servicemen were swept out to sea during one of the naval exercises due to a sudden deterioration in weather in the area, including strong winds. While rescue teams did manage to save three servicemen, the remainder were lost, their bodies recovered over the following days.
While President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared a day of mourning out of respect for the soldiers who passed away, criticism has hit the authorities hard, both regarding the accident and the subsequent approach by the authorities to the relatives of the deceased.
The accidental deaths prompted criticism at all levels of authority, not least in regards to how the tragedy was communicated to the relatives who were left behind. As news about the September 24 accident spread, relatives of servicemen involved in the exercise started to gather outside the Aktau morgue located close to the scene of the accident. There they sought answers regarding who was lost, demanding the names of those who had been identified.
Separated by a fence surrounding the morgue, military personnel later that day read out the names of the identified servicemen, most of whom were under the age of 25. The scene, which was captured on video and shared on social media, quickly gained attention for its impersonal and monotonous tone, with both activists and journalists calling out the authorities for handling the announcement in a way that was “Shocking [and] heartless.”
In the week following the accident, disciplinary actions were rolled out, with five officials from the Ministry of Defense being detained and put under investigation for their role in the accident. Among those detained were the chief of staff working with the naval forces, two military unit commanders, and a naval infantry company commander connected to the incident. The men are allegedly to blame for the accident due to negligence of service and violation of navigation rules, according to Kazakh police.
The incident did also force consequences at the highest levels of governance. Initially, Tokayev gave his condolences to the affected families and declared a day of mourning, to be observed on September 25. Days later, he sacked the minister of defense, Dauren Kosanov, who had been in the post just over 15 months. In his place, the now former commander of special operation forces, Aidos Myrzakhmetov, was appointed.
This is not the first accident of its kind. Four servicemen died as strong winds hit a military exercise in the same area of southwestern Kazakhstan in 2015. While this time the investigation and reshuffling of people connected to the Ministry of Defense might help prevent the recurrence of such accidents, military analyst Yermek Seitbattalov, whom the outlet Kaztag spoke to, still sees multiple shortcomings that the military has not fixed. The retired colonel, among other things, mentioned flaws in combat training and the preparation of officers, specifically in relation to the safety of servicemen during exercises. He said this issue was one of the most important matters of attention for the new defense minister.
The Kazakh authorities have shown themselves unequipped not only to properly communicate the passing of soldiers to their loved ones, but also to ensure the safety of those participating in military exercises. While Kazakhstan still mourns the tragedy, the test will be what the military learns from it.

articles.title: The Lingering Shadow of Rodrigo Duterte’s Drug War in the Philippines
articles.full_text:
The former Philippine president is on trial in The Hague, but the ghosts of his presidency and the system he put in place continue to haunt a deeply divided society.
Salvacion Ramos (left) and Llore Pasco (right) have remained in close contact every week since the deaths of their respective children, and are fighting for justice.
A few bags of chips and sweets line the modest storefront of Salvacion Ramos’ home in the Batasan neighborhood on the outskirts of Manila. At 68, she has turned the front of her house into a small convenience store to help pay for the education of her grandson, who has been in her care since her daughter’s death.
It was on that same doorstep one night in February 2017 that Cristeta Ramos was shot once in the back and three times in the head by four plainclothes police officers. “She died in my arms. I didn’t even get to say goodbye,” Salvacion recalls, tears in her eyes.
Beside her, her friend and neighbor Llore Pasco is also mourning her children. Her two sons, Cristanto and Juan Carlos, 34 and 31, were killed during a police operation as they were on their way to work in May 2017. “The police say they chased them because they thought they were thieves, but the bullet wounds were on the front of their bodies,” Llore says. She is now raising her five grandchildren.
“Cristeta was not a criminal” Salvacion says. “She did take drugs with the people she was with, but she wanted to get better. The barangay [neighborhood-level community] was offering a program for drug users to seek treatment, so I gave them her name.”
Llore’s sons had stopped using drugs well before Duterte’s election. After he took office, local officials insisted that former drug users register, presenting the process as a simple verification. Her sons initially refused. Llore eventually convinced them. They had been sober for more than a year. “Today I keep thinking that if they had not gone there, they might still be alive,” she says.
In neighborhoods across the country, barangays began compiling “watch lists” of current and former drug users. For some residents, getting off those lists came at a price. “At least five families I know paid 10,000 pesos (about $180) to the local government to get their names removed from the list, and their children are still alive,” Salvacion says.
Under Duterte, the war on drugs also became a source of income for some local actors. Along with the grief of losing their children and the guilt of having registered them with local authorities came the burden of paying to recover their bodies from the morgue. In Salvacion and Llore’s cases, authorities initially demanded 120,000 pesos and later 70,000 pesos, or about $1,350, after the intervention of the NGO Rise Up for Life and For Rights.
“Duterte destroyed these families, and now these mothers have to keep working to raise their orphaned grandchildren,” says Leah Valencia, a coordinator with the organization, which supports families in their search for justice.
Rise Up for Life and For Rights has also passed their testimonies to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, where Duterte has been held since his arrest in March 2025. The case accuses Duterte of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, during his time as mayor of Davao City and later as president. Prosecutors have identified 78 victims in the incidents specifically detailed in the case: 76 alleged murders and two attempted murders. The figure does not represent the total number of deaths attributed to Duterte’s drug war, but a selection of incidents presented by prosecutors to establish the alleged crimes against humanity.
The historic trial is scheduled to begin on November 30.
If Duterte is found guilty of crimes against humanity, he would become the first former president convicted by the ICC.
“The ICC is a very small ray of hope, but we are asking the government to turn Bato over and open an investigation to prosecute all those responsible,” Salvacion Ramos and Llore Pasco say together.
Duterte could soon be joined by his ally Senator Ronald dela Rosa, known as “Bato,” whom Duterte appointed chief of the Philippine National Police after he took office in 2016. In this capacity, dela Rosa oversaw the launch of “Double Barrel,” a cornerstone of the drug war that would leave about 30,000 people dead, according to estimates by several NGOs. (The official death toll of the police is around 6,000.)
On May 11, an attempt to arrest dela Rosa on a warrant for the ICC ended with him taking refuge inside the Philippine Senate as shots were fired in the building. The former police chief was placed under a form of protective custody inside the chamber before leaving the building a few days later. He is currently at large and wanted by Philippine authorities.
The fact that such chaos is possible reflects how politically sensitive the drug war remains at the highest levels of the Philippine state. In 2022, Duterte completed his single six-year term and was succeeded by Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son of the former dictator who ruled the country from 1965 to 1986, who was elected through an alliance with the Duterte camp. But the alliance did not last.
As relations between the two political clans deteriorated, Marcos gradually shifted his position on the International Criminal Court. In March 2024, he said the ICC had no authority to investigate the Philippines’ drug war and that his government would not cooperate with the court. Months later, as his alliance with the Dutertes unraveled, he adopted a softer stance, saying his government would not block an ICC investigation and would comply with its obligations to Interpol. By early 2025, his administration had also signaled that it was open to limited cooperation with the court.
Duterte was arrested by Philippine authorities, based on an Interpol Red Notice, at Manila’s airport on March 11, 2025.
While Marcos allowed police to enforce the ICC arrest warrant and accepted the presence of ICC investigators, he never openly opposed the drug war waged by his predecessor. He largely avoided the issue during the 2022 presidential campaign, particularly to preserve his alliance with the Duterte camp and its supporters.
He distanced himself from it only after taking office, when he promised a “bloodless” war on drugs. Joel Ariate, a social sciences researcher at the University of the Philippines and founder of the DAHAS project, which has tracked drug-war deaths since 2017, called the term “pure propaganda.”
“The Marcos government says there is no more blood being spilled. That is absurd. The drug war continues. The number of victims has dropped sharply, but there are still 200 to 300 deaths every year,” Ariate says. One-third of the victims are killed in police operations, he says, while the rest are mainly linked to private militias or hit men hired for less than $100 per killing.
The decline in violence against drug users could be a sign of progress under the Marcos government, but Ariate remains pessimistic. “Those responsible for thousands of killings, particularly low-ranking police officers, are still in their jobs. The police know the details and who took part,” the researcher says.
So far, only five cases have resulted in the conviction of nine police officers for crimes linked to Duterte’s drug war, according to a report from Human Rights Watch published in June this year. Yet DAHAS has documented many other cases in which police officers themselves filmed killings and posted the footage online as trophies.
Sitting in the university library where he works, Ariate shares his main concern. “In reality, the institutions that failed during the drug war have not changed,” he says. “In two years, there will be another presidential election, and if a politician like Duterte wins, it could all start again because the mentality has not changed either.”
In May 2025, two months after his arrest and transfer to The Hague, 63 percent of registered voters surveyed by Pulse Asia said they still trusted Duterte.
“Populist leaders present themselves as defenders of order and the fight against crime,” says Christopher Magno, a criminologist specializing in political violence and co-founder of the Truth Commission. “To justify their policies, they identify a group as responsible for insecurity: immigrants in the United States under Trump, and poor people and those accused of using or trafficking drugs in the Philippines under Duterte. By identifying an ‘enemy,’ they can legitimize a repressive policy and strengthen their popularity. Duterte therefore left office with very high levels of public support.”
The Truth Commission, established in 2026, is an independent body that brings together civilian experts from different fields, including law, forensic medicine, journalism, trauma-informed care, and education. Its work centers on collecting testimonies from victims and their families, preserving their stories, and examining the institutions and practices behind the drug war.
“Our goal is to document the facts and establish a truthful account, but above all to humanize the victims and begin a process of healing through a change in mentality,” Magno says.
The commission’s work is expected to last two years and be completed before the next elections, with findings released every six months. It offers new hope to victims’ families, though they remain cautious.
articles.summary: The former Philippine president is on trial in The Hague, but the ghosts of his presidency and the system he put in place continue to haunt a deeply divided society.

articles.title: The Woman Who Held Mahathir’s Hand For 70 Years
articles.full_text:
Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, who died this week aged 100, was a close companion of Mahathir throughout his long and tumultuous political career.
Former Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and his wife Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali attend Mahathir’s 100th birthday celebration at the Perdana Leadership Foundation in Putrajaya, Malaysia, July 10, 2025.
Dr. Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali had just one complaint about her husband, Dr. Mahathir Mohamad: that he was very shy about holding her hand in public. The man, who remained loyal and faithful to her for more than 70 years, felt a little embarrassed about showing his love for the Malay girl he met at King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore in 1947.
On Mahathir’s 93rd birthday, in an interview with Channel NewsAsia conducted by 10-year-old Kashika Selvam, Siti Hasmah narrated a funny incident about holding hands. She said that he was so shy that once, while driving through a highway toll booth, he pulled back his hand because he didn’t want the toll operator to see them holding hands.
Mahathir ruled Malaysia ruthlessly between 1981 and 2003, during which his critics and detractors were the subjects of sometimes furious political vendettas.
But when it comes to his fidelity and faithfulness to Siti Hasmah, even his critics cannot raise a finger against him.
At home, Mahathir was a loyal husband and an affectionate father, thanks in large part to Siti Hasmah. His daughter, Marina Mahathir, says her mother insisted that the siblings show their love and affection for each other openly by hugging and kissing.
Unlike many other politicians’ wives, Siti Hasmah’s conduct in public never gave a hint that she was the prime minister’s wife. Narrating a poignant incident in the 2019 documentary “M for Malaysia,” Siti Hasmah says: “I was taking my husband to the hospital, not the Prime Minister of Malaysia,” when Mahathir suffered a heart attack in 1989. Like any other devoted spouse, she was more concerned about her husband than the post he occupied.
Six years ago, on November 23, 2019, Malaysians saw a rare sight in Kuala Lumpur: the 94-year-old prime minister taking his 93-year-old wife out on a date. Driving Siti Hasmah in a Proton car, with no protocol or usual entourage, the couple went to a café on Jalan Bukit Bintang, where they had coffee and cake. It looked as if the two students who met at the medical college in Singapore were reliving those moments when they took a bus to Marine Parade to eat their favourite tauhu bakar, kangkong, and squid. The pictures touched such a chord with Malaysians that when Mahathir posted them on his official Instagram page, they received 55,000 likes and 2,000 comments.
Whenever the couple was asked about the secret of their marriage, both said in unison: tolerance. They married after a nine-year courtship. Both were in their thirties when they married. By that point, they were mature enough to understand each other’s goals in life. They never tried to portray themselves as the “perfect couple.” On many occasions, Siti Hasmah insisted that their marriage was like anybody else’s. There were happy moments and sad moments. They fought, made up and went on holidays together, she said.
Unlike others, there was nothing glamorous about this First Couple. They continued working towards their goals and made this marriage very endearing to Malaysians because they showed that accommodation and tolerance are a recipe for a lasting marriage.
On September 28, 2026, Siti Hasmah let go of Mahathir’s hand forever. On physical separation, Rumi once said: “Goodbyes are only for those who love with their eyes. Because for those who love with heart and soul there is no such thing as separation.” For 70 years, they were inseparable, and even death cannot separate them.

articles.title: Can Myanmar’s New Administration Revive the Stalled Dawei SEZ Project?
articles.full_text:
The flagship project struggled even during Myanmar’s decade of opening. Attempting to revive it amid conflict and sanctions will test its economic and strategic rationale.
A view of Dawei Myaun Yit pagoda in Dawei, Myanmar, May 31, 2018.
Myanmar’s military-backed administration is again trying to put the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) project on the agenda. This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone.
The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast.  It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance.
Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together.
The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.
Successive governments tried to address these constraints during Myanmar’s decade of political and economic opening. Myanmar and Thailand created a joint development vehicle in 2013, and Japan joined in 2015. Later, the government recast the Dawei project into initial and full phases. The first, smaller phase was estimated to cost about $1.7 billion. Financing remained difficult. In January 2020, under Myanmar’s elected civilian government, the Dawei SEZ Management Committee revised the concession terms to allow staged financing and reduce extra government risk.
By December 2020, it had terminated all nine initial-phase contracts with Italian-Thai Development after repeated delays and unmet financial obligations. The committee said the termination would allow it to rethink the project and seek new partners. The decision came just weeks before the February 2021 coup.
Dawei was hard to manage even when Myanmar had more access to international investors and development partners. Its problems with coordination and financing now exist in a much tougher economic, political, and security environment.
An ISP-Myanmar report based on official investment data shows recorded FDI falling from more than $28.7 billion in 2016-2020 to $7.4 billion in 2021-2025. Targeted post-coup sanctions remain in place, but the fall in investment reflects a wider deterioration that also includes armed conflict, policy uncertainty, difficult business conditions, and major corporate exits. Inflation and foreign-exchange pressure further complicate long-term investment.
The SEZ now effectively sits in a conflict zone. The fighting between military forces and local resistance groups has reportedly intensified around the project area, with reports of violence against civilians by military forces. The road toward Thailand crosses conflict-affected parts of Tanintharyi Region. The Htee Khee border trade area has also been controlled by the Karen National Union and its allied resistance forces since May 2025. For a cross-border SEZ, reliable access and security will remain central to long-term investment and development.
In this tougher setting, the Myanmar military-backed administration began making efforts to revive the project last year. Closer post-coup ties with Russia have brought Dawei back into active investment talks on power plants, oil refineries, and seaports. In June 2026, the Russian state-owned firm Inter RAO and the Myanmar military-controlled Launglon Economic Development Company signed an agreement for a 660-megawatt coal-fired power plant. Russia is seeking majority stakes during the project payback period to meet its banks’ lending conditions. The broader project plan is under discussion. Financing remains unsettled and undisclosed.
Beyond Russia, Dawei is reappearing in regional economic diplomacy. In August, Thailand also held bilateral talks on the Htee Khee-Dawei corridor under its policy of “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar. A month later, when coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Vietnam, Myanmar’s military-backed administration promoted Dawei to Vietnamese investors at a business forum in Hanoi. Dawei appears to be part of the new administration’s regional re-engagement talks, despite unresolved issues around financing, security, and implementation.
Alongside these challenges, the project’s revival raises concerns about its impact on local communities. A 2014 survey of more than 1,500 households reported concerns about land loss, limited consultation, and incomplete compensation. These concerns are now compounded by questions about ownership, transparency, environmental safeguards, and local benefits.
Dawei’s viability depends on more than building individual assets, but even that will be difficult under current conditions. The seaport, power plant, and transport links must support industry while also creating economic opportunities and benefits for communities. Without that wider ecosystem, Dawei could remain a scattered collection of infrastructure rather than a functioning and sustainable economic zone.

This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone.
The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast.  It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance.
Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together.
The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.
Successive governments tried to address these constraints during Myanmar’s decade of political and economic opening. Myanmar and Thailand created a joint development vehicle in 2013, and Japan joined in 2015. Later, the government recast the Dawei project into initial and full phases. The first, smaller phase was estimated to cost about $1.7 billion. Financing remained difficult. In January 2020, under Myanmar’s elected civilian government, the Dawei SEZ Management Committee revised the concession terms to allow staged financing and reduce extra government risk.
By December 2020, it had terminated all nine initial-phase contracts with Italian-Thai Development after repeated delays and unmet financial obligations. The committee said the termination would allow it to rethink the project and seek new partners. The decision came just weeks before the February 2021 coup.
Dawei was hard to manage even when Myanmar had more access to international investors and development partners. Its problems with coordination and financing now exist in a much tougher economic, political, and security environment.
An ISP-Myanmar report based on official investment data shows recorded FDI falling from more than $28.7 billion in 2016-2020 to $7.4 billion in 2021-2025. Targeted post-coup sanctions remain in place, but the fall in investment reflects a wider deterioration that also includes armed conflict, policy uncertainty, difficult business conditions, and major corporate exits. Inflation and foreign-exchange pressure further complicate long-term investment.
The SEZ now effectively sits in a conflict zone. The fighting between military forces and local resistance groups has reportedly intensified around the project area, with reports of violence against civilians by military forces. The road toward Thailand crosses conflict-affected parts of Tanintharyi Region. The Htee Khee border trade area has also been controlled by the Karen National Union and its allied resistance forces since May 2025. For a cross-border SEZ, reliable access and security will remain central to long-term investment and development.
In this tougher setting, the Myanmar military-backed administration began making efforts to revive the project last year. Closer post-coup ties with Russia have brought Dawei back into active investment talks on power plants, oil refineries, and seaports. In June 2026, the Russian state-owned firm Inter RAO and the Myanmar military-controlled Launglon Economic Development Company signed an agreement for a 660-megawatt coal-fired power plant. Russia is seeking majority stakes during the project payback period to meet its banks’ lending conditions. The broader project plan is under discussion. Financing remains unsettled and undisclosed.
Beyond Russia, Dawei is reappearing in regional economic diplomacy. In August, Thailand also held bilateral talks on the Htee Khee-Dawei corridor under its policy of “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar. A month later, when coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Vietnam, Myanmar’s military-backed administration promoted Dawei to Vietnamese investors at a business forum in Hanoi. Dawei appears to be part of the new administration’s regional re-engagement talks, despite unresolved issues around financing, security, and implementation.
Alongside these challenges, the project’s revival raises concerns about its impact on local communities. A 2014 survey of more than 1,500 households reported concerns about land loss, limited consultation, and incomplete compensation. These concerns are now compounded by questions about ownership, transparency, environmental safeguards, and local benefits.
Dawei’s viability depends on more than building individual assets, but even that will be difficult under current conditions. The seaport, power plant, and transport links must support industry while also creating economic opportunities and benefits for communities. Without that wider ecosystem, Dawei could remain a scattered collection of infrastructure rather than a functioning and sustainable economic zone.

articles.title: UN Refugee Agency Expresses Concerns About Malaysia’s Deportation of Asylum Seekers to Myanmar
articles.full_text:
The statement came as Kuala Lumpur confirmed plans to deport a further 3,500 people as part of its “voluntary repatriation program” with Myanmar.
Myanmar asylum seekers are escorted to Myanmar Navy vessels at Royal Malaysian Navy base, Sep. 29, 2026.
The United Nations refugee agency yesterday expressed its concerns over Malaysia’s return this week of nearly 1,500 asylum seekers to Myanmar, in spite of the ongoing conflict and dire humanitarian situation inside the country.
The 1,476 people were returned to Myanmar via ship on Tuesday, the first phase in the agreed “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 asylum seekers currently held in Malaysian immigration detention centers.
While Malaysia insists that the returns are strictly voluntary, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said yesterday that it was concerned about the fate of the 1,476 people, given the country’s continuing conflict and dire human rights and humanitarian situation.
Since those returned had been held in detention centers, it had “serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said in a statement. The U.N. agency has been blocked from accessing Malaysian immigration detention centers since 2019.
“We are concerned by these returns at a time when people sent back to Myanmar may face serious risks, and some within the group may be in need of international protection,” Wosornu said.
While recognizing Malaysia’s “sovereign responsibility” to manage asylum and migration issues, UNHCR urged the government “to ensure that all returns are subject to robust safeguards, including individual assessments and access to protection procedures.”
UNHCR’s statement came as Malaysia’s government confirmed that 3,524 refugees had been approved for the second phase of the “voluntary repatriation program.” Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said yesterday that the individuals had been identified by the Myanmar authorities, and that their names were submitted to Malaysia in a diplomatic note dated August 13. He added that Kuala Lumpur was awaiting notification from Myanmar on the date for the repatriation.
The ethnic make-up of the two groups is unclear, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has justified the repatriations with reference to the recent wave of public hostility towards the large population of Rohingya Muslims in Malaysia.
Thousands of Rohingya have arrived in Malaysia since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. As of February, Rohingya made up 126,000 of the 193,800 asylum seekers from Myanmar registered with UNHCR in Kuala Lumpur.
A coalition of civil society groups last week raised grave concerns about the possible deportation of Rohingya Muslims to Myanmar, given the continuing conflict in Rakhine State and the likelihood that they would be subjected to mistreatment and abuse.
Among ASEAN governments, Malaysia has been among the most critical of the Myanmar military’s seizure of power in 2021, and its ruthless attempts to put down the armed uprising that followed. But the growing domestic pressure over refugees has forced Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to adopt a more accommodating position toward Naypyidaw.
In a bid to expedite the return of refugees, Anwar is set to welcome coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia for an official visit later this month. Confirming the Myanmar leader’s visit yesterday, Communications Minister Fahmi said that Anwar would “hold discussions with Myanmar in the near future to facilitate the return of more Myanmar refugees to their country,” Bernama reported.
Given Malaysia’s previously principled position on Myanmar – to say nothing of its vocal advocacy for the Palestinian cause – rights groups have accused it of double standards.
“Malaysia has spoken forcefully about accountability, finding durable solutions, and the need to address the root causes of displacement in Myanmar,” Amnesty International Malaysia and Asylum Access Malaysia said in a statement yesterday. At the same time, it “is prepared to roll out the red carpet and host Min Aung Hlaing in Malaysia to facilitate the accelerated return of refugees.”
In response to these criticisms, Anwar has cited the need to prioritize the security and interests of Malaysia. “The issue of Myanmar refugees is not a new problem, but rather a legacy spanning decades that has placed pressure on the country in terms of security, social affairs and management,” he wrote in a Facebook post earlier this week.

articles.title: China’s Military Open New Logistics and Training Facility in Laos
articles.full_text:
The center north of Vientiane, a counterpart to a similar naval facility in Cambodia, marks a further extension of Beijing’s security presence in mainland Southeast Asia.
A satellite image shows the construction of the China-backed air strip in Ban Keun, Vientiane province, Laos, Jan. 3, 2026.
This week, the Chinese military opened a new logistics and training facility at an airport in Laos, further expanding its regional security presence and establishing the first overseas presence of the Chinese air force.
In a statement, China’s Ministry of Defense said that the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center was inaugurated on Tuesday, in a ceremony that was attended by Lao Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakaysone and a delegation from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
The facility, which is based at Ban Keun Airport, which sits close to the Nam Ngum River around 50 kilometers north of the capital Vientiane, also includes a China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
“The center, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots,” the Ministry said, but offered no details about what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport.
“The construction and use of the center reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, comply with both countries’ domestic laws, relevant international law and common practice,” it said. “It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability.”
Satellite imagery of the Ban Keun facility shows it also includes the construction of an extensive airfield. According to Reuters, work began on the new airfield in late 2025 and work was ongoing as of early September. “In place of green fields,” it reported, “a large paved runway and a parallel taxiway and apron were visible, along with a number of new buildings.”
The airport was built on the site of an airfield known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airstrips that were used by the U.S. military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, when the U.S. secretly supported an insurgency by anti-communist Hmong rebels. However, satellite images show that the new airfield expands far beyond the narrow, red-earthed strip established during the Vietnam War.
The new center adds to the handful of overseas facilities now operated by the PLA, since the opening of its first official overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017. It also complements a similar training and logistics facility that has been established at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand. The Cambodian facility was officially inaugurated by Prime Minister Hun Manet in April 2025, after three years of Chinese-funded refurbishments that include a 300-meter-long deep-water pier, a 5,000-ton dry dock, and a 1,000-ton slipway.
China’s involvement at Ream has attracted the suspicion of Western, and particularly American, security officials, who fear that the base may evolve into a full-blown Chinese base. Cambodia has sought to allay these fears by inviting foreign navies, including those of Japan, Vietnam, and the U.S., to visit the base.
Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said in a post on X that unlike Ream, the base in Laos is “more ostensibly similar to the one in Djibouti.” He added, “It may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA overseas base in Southeast Asia.”
The development at Ban Keun is perhaps unsurprising given the rapid expansion of China’s influence in Laos over the past 15 years. During that time, the north of the country has become economically fused to southern China, as new highways and an impressive China-built railway have improved overland connections. The Chinese investment presence is clearly visible in most parts of the country, and there is a large Chinese expatriate community in Vientiane and the provincial towns of northern Laos.
Defense relations have proceeded more slowly, perhaps due to the sensitivities of Vietnam, Laos’ traditional defense patron, which has had close ties with Laos dating back to the communist struggle of the 1960s and 1970s. In ⁠June, however, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing for meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which the two leaders agreed to enhance defense cooperation.
Xi also suggested that China and Laos should establish a “3+3” strategic dialogue mechanism involving their foreign, defense, and public security ministers, “as an opportunity to strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation and crack down on cross-border crimes.” (A similar mechanism was established with Cambodia earlier this year.) Last month, Beijing and Vientiane also concluded “Peace Train 2026,” a 16-day joint military exercise aimed at “humanitarian assistance and military medical services.”
One Chinese security analyst told the state-run Global Times that the base at Ban Keun was a means of providing the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force, which operates a small and obsolescent fleet of Chinese and Russian craft, with a “systematic training system for pilots, maintenance crew and flight personnel” that will reduce its reliance on overseas training. More broadly, the analyst said, the facility will deepen “practical exchanges” between the two militaries, “upgrading from simple equipment assistance to long-term integrated cooperation in talent training, joint exercises and equipment support.”
Perhaps most tellingly, the analyst drew an explicit parallel between Ban Keun and the facility at Ream Naval Base, noting that together they “cover inland airspace in the Indochina Peninsula and the maritime direction in the Gulf of Thailand.”
In both cases, the Chinese military has emphasized that the facilities have been established on the basis of “mutual respect” and are not directed at any
Nonetheless, the Ban Keun facility has the potential to alter the strategic map of mainland Southeast Asia, pulling Laos and Cambodia further out of the Vietnamese sphere of influence.
Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told Bloomberg that in light of the recent expansion of China’s military presence in Cambodia and the South China Sea, Vietnam in particular could have “serious grounds for concern” if the Ban Keun facility becomes a foothold for a more permanent PLA presence in Laos.
“These developments could give Beijing greater leverage over strategic access routes around Vietnam, raising concerns about its ability to monitor, and potentially constrain, Vietnam’s room for maneuver in time of crisis,” Giang told the newspaper. “Much depends on how the facility is used.”
Vietnam has not yet officially commented on the opening of the new facilities in Laos.

articles.title: Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
articles.full_text:
When the Gulf was last closed to tankers, Tokyo faced the same dilemma it faces today.
TOKYO, JAPAN – MAY 4TH 2016. JS 302 Tsushima Yaeyama-class minesweeper is open to the public in Tokyo Bay. The Tsushima was commisioned in 1993.
The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait, which is both the entrance to the Persian Gulf and one of the world’s most critical trade arteries. Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged, and the effects on daily life have been wide-ranging. The current crisis has a precedent. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to.
Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, beginning the Iran–Iraq War. Around 1984 the conflict spread to the sea, and passage through the Persian Gulf became hazardous for tankers as missile attacks and mines proliferated. In July 1987, at Kuwait’s request, the U.S. government dispatched warships and began escorting tankers, but a tanker still struck a mine. Washington then asked Western countries, including Japan, to send minesweepers. The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium all subsequently contributed to the minesweeping effort.
The Japanese government began exploring how it could contribute to navigational safety in the Gulf. Prime Minister Nakasone Yasuhiro was personally in favor of deploying personnel via MSDF minesweepers. On August 27, 1987, speaking before a Lower House committee, he argued that while he did not intend to order the dispatch, the act of removing mines would not, in his view, constitute the use of force, and that sending vessels to the Persian Gulf would not constitute the overseas dispatch of troops.
Naval mines constitute weapons of naval warfare, and laying them is an established means of naval combat. Under international law, minesweeping operations conducted during an armed conflict are themselves considered a use of force. This posed a legal challenge to Nakasone’s position: his argument applied only to the removal of abandoned mines in peacetime, after a ceasefire had been reached — not to active operations in an ongoing conflict.
Within the Japanese government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs led efforts to identify feasible forms of contribution. It became clear that any MSDF minesweeper dispatch would require a destroyer escort, and amid strong public opposition the government decided against sending minesweepers. Instead, it developed alternative proposals: providing economic cooperation in the Gulf region, sharing the costs of ensuring safe passage, increasing Japan’s host-nation support for U.S. forces, and dispatching JCG patrol vessels as a means of contributing personnel.
A senior Foreign Ministry official argued that dispatching JCG patrol vessels would circumvent constitutional constraints while signaling Japan’s proactive stance to the world. Under then Transport Minister Hashimoto Ryutaro, the Ministry of Transport and the JCG continued to explore this option. The JCG faced no statutory geographic limits on its activities, and operations in the Persian Gulf would have been legally permissible. The problem was operational: the Gulf was a war zone, and the safety of any JCG vessels deployed there could not be guaranteed.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Gotoda Masaharu would later describe Nakasone as one of the most outstanding postwar Japanese leaders, noting that they rarely differed in their political judgments — with one exception. That exception was the proposed dispatch of JCG patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf. Gotoda risked his position to oppose it, telling Nakasone that while the Cabinet would make the final decision, he personally would not sign off on it regardless.
Gotoda’s stand proved decisive. At U.S. urging, Japan instead agreed to fund the installation of high-precision radio navigation aids known as Decca chains. The resulting Decca Navigator stations allowed vessels to chart safe routes through the Gulf while avoiding the war zone, a practical and politically viable contribution that did not require deploying personnel into a combat area.
The 1987 episode established a precedent: Japan would not send vessels into an active conflict zone. That caution carried forward. Those 1987 deliberations directly shaped Japan’s approach to the subsequent Gulf War, and continue to shape its response to the current Strait of Hormuz crisis. During the Gulf War, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweepers to the Persian Gulf only after the ceasefire agreement took effect.
When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the U.S. again asked Japan to dispatch minesweepers and supply vessels. Senior Foreign Ministry officials resisted, citing the 1987 precedent against sending vessels into areas of armed conflict. Japan instead provided $13 billion in financial support, a contribution that drew a cold response from the international community, as it was widely viewed as checkbook diplomacy without strategic commitment. After the Gulf War ceasefire took effect in April 1991, with the Persian Gulf no longer a combat zone, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweeper units that same month. The pattern established in 1987 held: deployment was permissible, but only once hostilities had ceased. As Japan weighs its options in the current Strait of Hormuz crisis, that calculus — and the political constraints behind it — remain fundamentally　unchanged.

TSURUTA Jun is a professor at the Faculty of Law of Meiji Gakuin University.
articles.summary: When the Gulf was last closed to tankers, Tokyo faced the same dilemma it faces today.

articles.title: Who Is Russia’s New Ambassador to North Korea?
articles.full_text:
What can Andrei Podelyshev’s appointment tell us about North Korea-Russia relations?
Shortly after his arrival in Pyongyang, Russian Ambassador to North Korea Andrei Podelyshev pays respects at the memorial honoring North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces, Sep. 26, 2026.
Russia has finally filled the ambassadorial post in Pyongyang, which had sat vacant for nearly eight months. Under a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on July 28, career diplomat Andrei Podelyshev – at the time, Russia’s ambassador to Nigeria, a post he had held since December 2024 – was named the new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. A companion decree released him from his Nigerian posting the same day.
Podelyshev arrived in Pyongyang nearly two months later, on September 26, together with his wife, aboard a direct Nordwind flight from Moscow. According to the Russian Embassy and TASS, he headed straight from the airport to the Soviet-era Liberation Monument to pay tribute to fallen Red Army soldiers, before visiting Pyongyang’s newly built memorial complex for North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces in Kursk.
Podelyshev is, on paper, one of the more genuinely “Korea-literate” diplomats Moscow could have sent. He graduated from MGIMO (the Moscow State Institute of International Relations) in 1984 and joined the Soviet Foreign Ministry that same year. He speaks both English and Korean, and over his career he has served at the Soviet embassy in Pyongyang itself, as well as at Russian missions in South Korea and the United States.
What stands out, though, is the decade he spent away from Asia desks entirely. From 2005 to 2015, Podelyshev was deputy director of the Consular Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, the branch of the ministry responsible for visas, citizenship matters, and the movement of foreign nationals in and out of Russia.
That background is not a minor biographical footnote. Consular policy has become one of the most sensitive, and most scrutinized, levers of the entire North Korea-Russia relationship. Since 2022, Russian consular services have issued tens of thousands of visas to North Korean citizens, the overwhelming majority formally classified as “educational” visas. 
According to Russia’s own data, the number of visas issued to North Koreans jumped from 9,239 in 2024 to 36,413 in 2025, with 35,849 of them, over 98 percent, nominally for education. Investigations by NK Pro and others have shown that these “student” visas are routinely used by Russian firms to bring in North Korean laborers while sidestepping United Nations Security Council Resolution 2375, which bars U.N. member states from issuing work permits to North Korean nationals.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, an 11-country group tracking sanctions evasion, went further in a report released September 16, 2026, stating, “The Russian government has created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students,” including workers employed in drone manufacturing at Russian defense-industrial sites such as the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan The report estimates that 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean laborers were working in Russia by the end of 2025, each generating roughly $7,500 a year in wages – up to five times what similar labor earns in China.
Sending an ambassador with nearly a decade of consular-management experience to preside over an embassy now processing this volume of visa traffic is unlikely to be a coincidence. Whether or not Podelyshev personally shaped this scheme during his 2005-2015 tenure at the Consular Department, he has strong professional grounding in the visa categories, documentation, and institutional workarounds that have made the “student visa” loophole possible in the first place.
The post of Russia’s envoy to North Korea had been empty since the death of Aleksandr Matsegora, who served as ambassador from December 2014 until December 6, 2025, when he died in Pyongyang at age 70. Matsegora, also an MGIMO graduate, held the job for just over a decade, the longest tenure of any foreign ambassador to North Korea, and was present for the relationship’s most consequential turning points, including hosting the reception marking the entry into force of the June 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
Matsegora’s profile was that of an Asia-desk veteran who rose through the ministry’s regional bureaucracy. His successor, Podelyshev, combines an earlier Korea specialization with a mid-career detour into consular administration and, most recently, a comparatively low-profile ambassadorship in Nigeria. He is not one of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s marquee Asia strategists; he is more of a technocrat suited to managing an embassy whose day-to-day workload – handling visas, labor migration, and logistics – has expanded dramatically alongside the military relationship.
Unlike the politically weighted appointments Russia sometimes makes to signal priority, Podelyshev is not a front-rank figure in shaping strategy toward Pyongyang. His nomination reads as a bet on administrative competence, someone who can run the visa pipeline and consular relationship, at a moment when the institution-building phase may be giving way to a more routine, logistics-heavy phase of the alliance.
Podelyshev will oversee the continued evolution of the deepest North Korea-Russia alignment since the Cold War. Since the 2024 security treaty was signed, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia retake Kursk, along with supplying Russia’s military with munitions and ballistic missiles. South Korean intelligence estimates that North Korea has deployed over 16,000 troops to Russia since October 2024, alongside more than 15 million artillery rounds supplied. The United States estimates that Pyongyang earned somewhere from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion through 2025 for its military assistance to Russia. Cooperation continues, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that North Korea is preparing to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia.
Podelyshev’s first public act, honoring both Soviet World War II dead and North Korean Kursk casualties on the same day, signaled Moscow’s intent to frame today’s military alignment as the natural extension of a Soviet-era blood bond, rather than as a wartime marriage of convenience.
But before Podelyshev arrived, Moscow left the Pyongyang post unfilled for nearly eight months, even during the most intense period of military cooperation in the relationship’s history. The extended vacancy suggests that the strategic decisions binding the two countries are being made elsewhere — through the direct leaders’ channel and military-intelligence links, rather than through the embassy itself.
